This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies within containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops continuously audits a program's system calls and builds upon a rules-based language to create and manage a set of temporal rules. These rules enable Timeloops to predict future legitimate system calls, allowing it to create a reduced filter for the program's secure operation. We demonstrated the effectiveness of Timeloops by applying it to the evaluation of temporary system data persistence and verified its performance on various benchmark tests. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of Timeloops is made available for others to use and review. We found that, on average, the learning and prediction capabilities of Timeloops result in a 30% more compact system call filter, compared to an optimal static solution, with only a 10% increase in processing time. Additionally, the review of our code by other researchers yielded no security vulnerabilities. We discovered that, with the help of Timeloops, the system call learning module for the Apache HTTP Server could be optimized from 22MB to 13MB in size. This optimized version has since been incorporated into the official Apache HTTP Server codebase. The ultimate resolution of Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) is constrained by the spherical aberration coefficient, which significantly impairs the achievement of sub-pico-meter resolution.  This restriction can be overcome by employing a device capable of compensating for spherical aberration, however implementing such a device in the electron microscope's image formation system is extremely difficult.  This paper introduces a novel electronic phase disc that can be programmably optimized to counteract the effects of spherical aberration by producing a distorted electron wave function in the backscatter mode.  The disc's functionality can be easily adjusted through the incorporation of an additional electron beam, which facilitates profound image enhancement.  Our findings indicate that this simple yet effective solution can provide nearly ideal point-spread functions, markedly enhancing the TEM's resolution to a level where atomic-scale analysis becomes feasible.  Furthermore, this technique can also be employed to develop custom-designed point-spread functions, facilitating multiple image reconstruction techniques, including Fourier-based methods and blind reconstruction.  The effectiveness of this approach is verifiable through the execution of a Monte Carlo simulation.  This novel electronic phase disc can be incorporated into both TEMs and Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopes (S/TEMs).  Additionally, this research introduces a novel application entitled the Electronic Disc Designer, an interactive tool that enables users to create customized electronic discs tailored to specific spherical aberration coefficients.  This technology can also be adapted for use in Electron Microscopy Simulation Library (EMSL).  This paper provides a thorough explanation of the electronic disc's functionality, design details, along with simulations and actual test images obtained using a custom-designed electronic disc in a TEM.  The incorporation of this novel electronic disc can provide optimal image quality and facilitate atomic-scale analysis in the electron microscope.  This technology may also serve as a foundation for the development of novel electron microscopy techniques. The success of data-driven conversation models largely relies on their ability to encode input information and generate relevant output. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its quality and realism, the underlying representation of input text is not as widely examined. Our study delves into analyzing the encoder representations of two popular conversation models in a generative setting, specifically the Transformer-based BART and a bidirectional encoder based on the BART architecture. We observed that the embeddings extracted from the final layer of these models often contained sufficient task-related information when compared to a stronger, multi-task trained encoder. However, this information content seemed to decline as the number of layer depths increased. Our findings suggest that pre-training conversation data in a generative manner may not effectively pass relevant information to the encoder representations, which could have implications for conversations starting with unknown input. On the other hand, using a stronger, naturally bidirectional encoder resulted in more nuanced understanding of the input text, which we demonstrated through both a quantitative analysis of text classification and a qualitative examination of generated examples. Our study provides a comprehensive examination of both encoder architectures and training data, which can guide researchers in identifying promising paths to enhancing the understanding of conversation models. Our study specifically explores two conversation models, but the evaluation framework we introduced is more broadly applicable to any language generation models. In this research, we examine the behavior of Q-balls in multiple scalar theories both analytically and numerically, focusing on situations that arise in certain cosmological scenarios known as 'dynamical Q-ball generation'. Our analysis reveals that, unlike simple SUSY models, Q-balls in multiple scalar theories can exhibit a unique feature - they can undergo a transition from a solid 'homogeneous' structure to a 'cored' one. Furthermore, our findings suggest that such cored structures can actually become more stable than their homogeneous counterparts under certain conditions. Additionally, we found that the density of the Q-ball's core can be quite high, which could have implications for its behavior in certain situations. The study of Q-balls in multiple scalar theories can provide valuable insights into the phenomenon of dynamical Q-ball generation, and therefore is an important area of study. In this work, we explore the concept of computable functions applied to infinite strings, focusing on Turing-computable strings which form a computably enumerable set. We aim to establish the existence of a computably creative function that generates infinite strings from any given input, a concept closely related to the fundamental theorem concerning the existence of a computably infinite set containing all computably finite sets as subsets. This investigation applies to both partial and total functions, with the latter being equivalent to a computable function on finite strings with an infinite output. We also introduce the idea of computably creative functions for multiple inputs and a computably selective function that produces a finite output for any infinite input, also exploring its relationship with a computably creative function for finite strings. These findings extend our understanding to include a computably selective function for strings with a specific computable property, such as being a Turing degree. Finally, we discuss how a computably selective function can be used to create a computably creative function on infinite strings with a specific computable output, such as a particular letter or a letter alternating between two options. This, in turn, enables the creation of a computably selective function for any Turing degree, ultimately leading to the demonstration of a computably creative function that can output any computably enumerable infinite string. Deep neural network models, regardless of their extensive performance in various tasks, often rely heavily on global representations of input data and struggle to capture local aspects. This limitation is particularly evident in tasks that involve understanding spatial relationships within images or temporal dynamics in sequences. To overcome this, we introduce a novel, recurrent activation function design called Modulated Recurrent Activation (MRA). This novel activation function builds on the foundation of the laid-out, factored design of Local Response Normalization and implements a similar, efficient computation that modulates both the derivative and the value of the recurrent unit. By integrating an additional learned component, we enhance the activation function to conserve the original data's dynamic range. We employed MRA within a customized, local pooling component called the Local Recurrent Activation Unit (LRAU) which we successfully applied to several deep network configurations for image recognition, sequential analysis, and video analysis. Our results indicate that LRAUs not only significantly reduce the quantity of parameters required but also yield state-of-the-art performance in comparison to existing methods. Moreover, our analysis reveals that LRAUs facilitate a more interpretable analysis of temporal dynamics through the conservation of a data-specific range. We are the first to introduce a modular, trainable component that can extract local features from input data, making our activation function a versatile resource for the community. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as Multiple-Choice Knowledge Promption (MCKP), which employs interactive multiple-choice queries to facilitate cross-task generalization.
The proposed method draws on both high-frequency knowledge and rare task-specific information to guide the model's improvement, with subsequent enhancements achieved via both inter-task and intra-task retrieval augmenting.
Our results indicate that the proposed method yields significant enhancements in zero-shot and few-shot settings, with further gains from additional iterations.
Moreover, MCKP proves effective for both single-model and ensemble scenarios, showcasing its practical applicability.
With multiple experiments and detailed analysis, we provide insight into the effects of various MCKP components and the inherent robustness of the proposed framework. 
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/mckp for reference and use.

In our research, we investigated the challenges of hyperparameter optimization for private machine learning models by incorporating a private component. Our analysis revealed that the stabilization mechanism of dropouts and batch normalization significantly reduces the optimal hyperparameter values necessary for accurate prediction, thereby making them less susceptible to optimization. Moreover, our findings show that adding noise to the batch axis has a confined impact on hyperparameters, whereas the optimal values for learning rate and dropout are largely independent of the private hyperparameter setup. Our analysis also revealed that a broad initial search range for the private hyperparameter is essential to ensure accurate selection. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed framework for the selection of private hyperparameters, which outperformed the current methods by achieving up to 12% improvement in test accuracy for self-supervised learning and 5% improvement in test accuracy for regular supervised learning. Our framework's superiority was confirmed across multiple private deep learning setups, learning environments, and models. Our code is available at https://github.com/aleksamelnikov/PrivateHyperparameterTuning. We establish a natural correspondence between boolean structures and specific subsets of generators within these groups, establishing a connection that holds universally. We then focus on the case of finite non-Abelian groups, determining their equivalence to boolean structures generated by their 2-rank. We, however, find that not all finite non-Abelian groups can be expressed as the generator sets of other groups, indicating that our universal connection holds only up to a particular morphism. We also establish an algebraic definition for the boolean structures associated with groups, using the concept of boolean identities, and explore its implications for various classical groups, demonstrating that many of these groups are equivalent to the associated boolean structures. We further consider the category of boolean structures connected to group generators, examining its algebraic and categorical properties, and we identify the natural morphisms within this category as being determined by the group homomorphisms, inducing a categorical structure on the collection of these boolean structures. We also explore the representation of boolean structures in a categorical sense, using the concept of a boolean functor, and demonstrate that this functor establishes a correspondence between groups and their associated boolean structures, a connection that holds due to the universal nature of the boolean structures. We, however, face a limitation in extending this connection to a functor that is categorical in nature, primarily because some groups do not have unique generator sets. We discuss two potential paths for overcoming this constraint, involving either the introduction of additional structure to the groups or a more flexible definition of the boolean structures, and we examine the implications of such changes on the connections between the groups and the associated boolean structures. We also explore the concept of modifying the boolean structures to make them categorically equivalent, a change that would, however, alter their original structure. We, however, find that the ability to consistently define such modified boolean structures across all groups would require the adherence to a specific axiom that would, however, be violated, indicating that such a consistent definition is impossible. We then discuss the broader implications of our findings within the context of category theory and group theory, and we examine the connections between the boolean structures and other mathematical structures, such as lattices, exploring the possibilities of generalizing our results to these structures. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in January 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, where social distancing measures and lockdowns were implemented to contain the virus' transmission. As online rumors continued to circulate and contribute to harmful actions among citizens, the Chinese government intensified efforts to combat them. As a technical contribution, we developed a social network-based approach to analyzing and predicting the dissemination of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 outbreak. Our method combines linear diffusion and intuitive targeting to model the spread of misinformation and predicts the likelihood of a user sharing a rumor based on their willingness to do so. This prediction framework leverages features from Twitter and Weibo data that capture users' behaviors and characteristics. Our analysis of Chinese users' behavior revealed key factors that influence the spread of information, specifically time-dependent characteristics of online communities, where the speed of rumor dissemination accelerates during peak online hours and slows down at night. Our evaluation of the effectiveness of the Chinese government's disinfection services also showed that targeted efforts are more effective than non-targeted approaches in reducing the dissemination of online rumors. Furthermore, our study found that a 1% increase in willing users leads to a 2.35% increase in the spread of a rumor, and that a 1% improvement in disinfection services results in a 2.33% reduction in the rumor's reach. Our solution has the potential to address other online diffusion challenges and complex propagation issues in social networks. Our research was conducted in partnership with Weibo's data providers, who confirmed our approach's validity and suggested its utility in predicting and controlling the spread of online rumors in China. Our study has implications for the ongoing battle to contain the COVID-19 pandemic and other global health crises, as well as future social challenges that involve complex problem-solving in multi-agent systems. Our work has been recognized with the Best Paper Award at the 2019 IEEE Conference on Computational Information Systems. Despite its achievements, our research has several limitations, primarily resulting from the restrictions imposed by Weibo that prevented us from collecting a larger dataset. As a result, our study is primarily representative of users in China's online community. Furthermore, our approach relies on linear diffusion models, which may not capture the complex underlying mechanisms that give rise to the spread of information in social networks. This method, which eliminates the need for traditional nebulae template spectra, involves identifying characteristic absorption features in planetary nebulae spectra to establish a relative scale of distances. As a result, a uniform distance measure has been derived for the Fornax cluster galaxies using this method, yielding a distance of 17.95 megaparsecs (3 sigma uncertainty: 0.03). The traditional method using surface brightness fluctuations yields a comparable distance of 17.78 megaparsecs (3 sigma uncertainty: 0.03). It also includes a comprehensive data set on the properties of planetary nebulae, including dimensionless distances, radial velocities, and apparent brightess. This paper explores certain non-degenerate curves in a semi-Riemannian space of dimension $n\geq 3$, specifically those with acceleration vector $X$ that is tangent to itself. We establish that these curves can be classified into two categories: those with an acceleration vector that is a linear combination of its own past and future images, resulting in an integral curve of an optimal mapping $\phi$, and those that do not fit this criterion. We refer to the former as weakly stable curves and demonstrate that they maintain a constant acceleration vector. Moreover, we derive a consistent optimal mapping $\phi$ for weakly stable curves, defined by $X=\phi'$. Conversely, we prove that any curve with an acceleration vector that is an integral curve of an optimal mapping $\phi$ is a weakly stable curve, specifically a Timelike Bertrand curve. We further establish that in a flat space, these curves are lines or hyperplanes. We also discuss various examples and demonstrate that the acceleration vector of a Timelike Bertrand curve is preserved when the curve is mapped through a homothety or a rotation. Lastly, we provide a definition for weakly stable surfaces and show that these define an integral submanifold for an optimal mapping $\phi$. We also derive the equation for a Timelike Bertrand surface in an Euclidean space. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between these curves and surfaces and certain established concepts, specifically how they are related to optimal mappings, rank-$1$ differential operators, and conformal geometry. This research investigates the underlying reasoning for this practice, suggesting that loss function modifications can lead to inconsistent test set performance, dependent on factors like model size and dataset characteristics. Our findings reveal that loss function modifications can result in models that memorize dataset patterns over features, causing a performance drop when switching to a more challenging test set. Additionally, we found that the optimal model size varies based on the loss function and dataset features, further contributing to inconsistent results. To address these concerns, this research introduces a robust evaluation framework that assesses deep learning models based on their intrinsic classification capability, unaffected by external factors, by utilizing a surrogate model that predicts loss values. This framework enables the fair comparison of models using different loss functions, such as the original cross-entropy loss, by standardizing the prediction scores through normalization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by evaluating the performance of models trained with modified loss functions, such as the focal loss, on the FlowNet dataset, showing that the results are robust to changes in model architecture. Furthermore, this research facilitates the selection of optimal model parameters by integrating the proposed framework with a simultaneous search algorithm, leading to the identification of exceptional models capable of achieving low loss values on both the training and validation sets, along with enhanced performance on the test set. New modeling of neutron-star collapses, incorporating advanced numerical simulations of rotating neutron stars, reveals that gravitational wave emission is generated by a neutron star's core collapse. The new framework surpasses the simplicity of the single-dimensional fluid model and better captures the neutron star's dynamics. However, this more sophisticated model also increases uncertainties in the signal detection process, as the new framework predicts waveforms that may not be unique to specific events. As a result, the detection of gravitational waves from a supernova-induced black-hole formation event might require more sensitive detectors and more comprehensive searches of signal templates. Furthermore, the new framework raises questions about the possibility of identifying the supernova's multi-messenger signs, such as a bright electromagnetic counterpart, which could be linked to the gravitational wave signal's characteristics. We examine the possible relationships between gravitational wave signals and the accompanying electromagnetic radiation, including the effects of neutron star spin, orientation, and the presence of an accompanying black hole in mergers. We also discuss the implications of these connections for future multi-messenger searches. We find that a discovery of a gravitational wave signal with an identifiable electromagnetic counterpart would provide strong evidence for the new framework's models and possibly even the identification of a specific event. Conversely, the failure to detect such a counterpart from a signal consistent with the new framework would imply that our current understanding of supernova physics is incorrect. This study expands on that finding by examining the influence of water within these temperature ranges, given that water plays a crucial role in protoplanetary discs and can significantly affect planetary formation processes. When particles with water content (approximately 0.7 wt. %) were subjected to the same conditions as before, we observed that the shift from brittle to sticky behavior at 1000 K remains a key factor in particles' physical properties. Notably, an analogous Inagaki experiment, replicated with our setup and using a higher water content (around 2.4 wt. %), produced results that, despite some discrepancies, still support the idea that temperature influences the sticking phenomenon over a specific range. Furthermore, we propose that the interval of temperature variability in protoplanetary discs, which is generally thought to be in the range of 700-1100 K, could be crucial in determining the sticking characteristics of forming planets, and that this influence could be reflected in the composition of chondritic meteorites. This research provides valuable insights that can be used to model the sticking behavior of particles in protoplanetary discs more accurately, which is essential for understanding planetary formation processes. We also highlight the importance of conducting further experiments with a focus on temperature ranges that are harder to replicate in the lab, such as those below 600 K, as well as exploring other factors that influence the sticking behavior of particles. This could involve examining the impact of various liquids on particles' physical properties, or the influence of different impact velocities on bond formation. This would enable a more comprehensive modeling of particle behavior in protoplanetary discs and a deeper understanding of planetary formation processes. In an increasingly complex robotics environment, leveraging mimicry learning is crucial for efficient and fast policy training. Our research extends conventional mimicry learning through adapted imitation, adherence to linear constraints, and navigation around obstacles. By utilizing a robust loss function that incorporates multiple loss types, we demonstrate significant improvements in performance. Our work also eliminates the need for explicit reward function definition. The improved policy training is accomplished via a dense reward function learned from observed outcomes associated with specific actions in a sampling environment. This learned reward function aids in accounting for linear constraints and obstacle avoidance. Our method is evaluated in multiple scenarios with satisfying results. An additional contribution is the release of six new scenarios designed to assess the efficacy of mimicry learning methods. These scenarios are distinct from the three previously developed environments by including narrow passages, complex static obstacles, linear constraint conditions, and areas that require full crossing. Our research indicates that the proposed EKMP method exceeds the performance of conventional mimicry learning methods in every environment tested. The advantages of our approach are further highlighted through the comparison of its simple and efficient implementation to more complex policy gradient methods. The achievements of the proposed EKMP method are also shown to be compatible with multiple different action probability distribution parameters. Our work also includes the development of an interactive tool that allows the visual inspection of policy trajectory maps in multiple environments. This tool enables the detection of areas that may pose difficulties for multiple mimicry learning methods. With the proposal of the EKMP method, and the development of an evaluation suite that includes six new challenging scenarios, we have created a foundation for exploring a broader range of mimicry learning methods capable of handling complex constraints and obstacle avoidance through adapted imitation. The name of this research area is defined as Extended Kernelized Mimicry Policy (EKMP) learning. One potential direction for future research is to investigate the application of a variety of different kernel functions that could further improve the performance of kernelized mimicry learning methods. The initial evaluation of the proposed research is positive, indicating that the proposed approach outperforms conventional mimicry learning in every environment tested. Additionally, the results show that the proposed EKMP method excels in complex static obstacle avoidance scenarios due to its unique formulation that meets linear constraint conditions through the use of a hyperplane that originates from the sampling environment. This Rashba interaction, originating from lateral shell or surface contributions, forms a gap in the Rashba Hubbard model's spectrum and facilitates the realization of a topological superfluid phase through the manipulation of a Ginzburg-Landau order parameter. Moreover, this particular superfluid phase exhibits unique characteristics, such as a non-zero Majorana-Zee-Koshnode and Weyl points within the superfluid's spectrum, their intersection signaling the onset of topological superfluidity. This theoretical framework is grounded in numerical simulations of Rashba Hubbard models using a Ginzburg-Landau theory near half-filling. Our findings suggest that spin-singlet topological superfluidity can be implemented using magnetic field-tuned Rashba interaction in anatomic system, specifically in Cu$_{x}$Bi$_{2}$Se$_{3}$. This technique allows for the experimental identification of topological superfluidity through optical detection of atomic motion and/or transport experiments. A particular magnetic field value can serve as a threshold, switching between the normal state and the spin-singlet topological superfluid state. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state in the type II superconductor Tl-2201, characterized by a vortex lattice structure of intersecting squares. This novel arrangement occurs when the magnetic field is slightly below the necessary strength to enter the perpendicular direction's normal state. A theoretical model suggests that at this point, an alternating pattern of square and triangular vortex lattices exists, with the squares dominating in areas where the magnetic field is closer to the parallel state. This model also predicts that in regions where the perpendicular state is present, a triangular vortex lattice structure will prevail. These predictions are supported by our measurements of the sound wave velocity and absorption in these intermediate magnetic field strengths. Moreover, the rotation of both the square and triangular vortex lattices with increasing magnetic field strength is evident in our measurements of the sound wave velocity and absorption. This finding provides us with a unique opportunity to study the physics of these two lattice structures in close proximity and may pave the way for the investigation of other transition states in complex superconverting systems. Additionally, the conditions necessary for these two lattice structures to exist could be useful for the realization of new types of electrodynamic hidden order states in certain types of superconductive materials. The model we developed for these situations could also be applicable to the study of other multi-state transition phenomena in strong magnetic fields. Theories explaining polymer dynamics are typically developed with reference to idealized, stretched bristles, however these models often fail to account for the excluded volume of the polymer chains, leading to an incomplete understanding of polymer behavior in various extensions. This study builds upon existing theories by considering a broad class of strongly stretched, melted polymers with spatially varying shapes, and demonstrates that the excluded volume effect diminishes as the polymer is stretched further, ultimately leading to a finite "exclusion zone" around the polymer's tip. This phenomenon results in an asymmetrical distribution of polymer end points, with implications for the mapping of bristle shapes and the scaling of polymer properties with changing stretch levels. Furthermore, this study identifies conditions under which the exclusion zone becomes a fixed shape, similar to that of a stretched ellipse, and confirms the associated scaling of bristle properties through numerical simulations. The proposed framework bridges the gap between existing theories and provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of strong, melted polymers. This knowledge may also be applied to facilitate the mapping of bristle shapes, helping to bridge the gap between molecular behavior and Bragg grating bristle metrology. This combined approach provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of strong, melted polymers, and could also be used to map bristle shapes through an extension of our theoretical model that includes data fitting parameters. This framework is particularly relevant to the measurement of melted polymers, such as dendrimers and biopolymers, where Bragg grating bristle microscopy offers a non-invasive means of assessing their physical properties. The serial dictatorship method determines the winner by sequentially deciding on one option at a time, retroactively eliminating previous choices. We explore possible improvements to this method in the context of choosing one item from a set where others have similar preferences. Specifically, we examine two potential upgrades: first, introducing a new preferred item to influence decisions, and second, allowing decision-makers to weigh the importance of different items. We establish conditions under which either of these variants offers a more equitable outcome than the standard serial dictatorship approach. This involves applying the Gross-Soave theorem and interpreting the results in the context of preference aggregation. Ultimately, we identify scenarios in which the enhanced versions consistently outperform the standard method. This involves defining a suitable metric for assessing decision-making methods and demonstrating that neither the standard nor the enhanced methods yield the most optimal results in every scenario. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to examine the impact of introducing a new preferred item on the outcome of social choice methods. This includes investigating what it means for a method to perform best overall and identifying conditions under which the standard serial dictatorship method is superior to alternative social choice methods. This knowledge contributes valuable insights to the broader theory of social choice. We also explore possible generalizations for further research. This involves scrutinizing the underlying assumptions of the standard serial dictatorship method and identifying areas where there is scope for enhancing decision-making processes. We apply a suite of sophisticated mathematical tools to tackle complex theoretical questions. This involves using a range of advanced theoretical concepts, including but not limited to, graph theory, game theory, and topological properties, to derive results and prove the validity of various social choice methods. We successfully demonstrate the efficacy of the enhanced serial dictatorship methods, by: first, formally defining the conditions under which the standard serial dictatorship method is inferior; second, deriving precise outcomes for a variety of social choice scenarios; third, providing clear and concise conditions for optimal performance in social choice scenarios; and lastly, accurately generalizing conditions for optimal performance in social choice scenarios. We designed two distinct detection strategies to identify binary asteroids by analyzing archival images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey.  Firstly, we created a predictive model for determining the shape of main belt asteroids by analyzing the fluctuations in their light curves in different color bands. This approach allowed us to identify potential binary asteroids by comparing our findings to existing observations and taking into account the characteristics of the orbiting objects as they reflect light in different colors. Secondly, we constructed a statistical model to estimate the number of main belt asteroids based on their maximum brightness, and used this model to narrow down our search in the Pan-STARRS1 images. This model helped us pinpoint 27 possible binary asteroids by analyzing nearly 700 thousand observations of the main belt asteroids. We further verified these findings by analyzing the observed fluctuations in the light curves of these 27 possible binary asteroids and comparing them to a group of known binary asteroids. Our study revealed that about 3 to 8 percent of the main belt asteroids that shine brightly enough to be detected by Pan-STARRS1 are likely to be binary asteroids. We also found that in certain orbit paths around the Sun, known as orbital paths, the proportion of binary asteroids is significantly higher, at about 20 to 30 percent, or in some cases as low as one to two percent. The exact percentage varies depending on the specific orbital path.  Furthermore, our study included an inventory of the narrow-belt asteroids and identified several possible binary asteroids in different orbital paths, particularly in the orbital paths that cross the path of the Earth around the Sun known as the intersection zones.  Additionally, we discovered that the binary asteroids we found in the image analysis move in the galaxy's plane, except for one asteroid known as 72039 2000 YB5.  Its unusual path may be the result of being affected by the gravitational pull of the planet Venus due to their close proximity to each other.  We also found that several possible binary asteroids in the narrow-belt area, such as 87184 2001 XN85 and 87954 2000 YK49, have an irregular shape similar to that of the asteroid 617 Patroclus, a known binary asteroid in the broad-belt area. The Southern Atlantic rift system exhibits asymmetrical geometry, with pronounced variations in crustal thickness and continental margin types. Despite this, there has not been an in-depth analysis of the system's kinematics and crustal accumulation processes. Using a detailed model of plate motion and thermal evolution, we simulated the Southern Atlantic rifting process from 1300 km of extension at a rate of 1.5-2 km/year. The modeling reveals that symmetric and asymmetric modes of rifting alternative, depending on the temperature of the mantle. Low mantle temperatures result in rifting modes I and II, characterized by echelon-shaped faults and arrays of NNE-trending conjugate faults respectively. Conversely, high mantle temperatures produce rifting mode III, with radial arrays of faults, resembling those found in Iceland. The modeling also indicates that in order to prevent the break-up of Africa and South America, rifting in these areas needed to occur at different times, with extended periods of pre-rift crust in Africa allowing it to withstand more extension before breaking up. The models further show that in order to explain the observed variations in continental margin types, the Southern Atlantic rift system had to switch between different modes of rifting, with the Volva Basin representing the transition from rifting mode I to mode II, and the Walvis and Brasilia Basins representing the transition from II to III. The modeling also predicts that radial rifting modes should result in continental margin types with high crustal accumulation, such as the passive Atlantic margins of Europe and North America. Conversely, rifting modes I and II should result in continental margin types with low crustal accumulation, such as the South Atlantic conjugate passive margins found in Brazil and South Africa. These predictions are confirmed by seismic data, where the conjugate passive margins in Brazil and South Africa display low crustal accumulation, and the extended and thinned Atlantic margins in Europe and North America display high crustal accumulation. The modeling also indicates that radial rifting modes should result in cratons being broken up into two separate pieces, such as the break-up of the Kaapvaal and Pilbara Cratons, whereas asymmetric and asymmetric rifting modes should result in cratons sticking to the edge of, such as the break-up of the Congo Craton. The modeling further shows that radial rifting modes should result in lithosphodic extension, and asymmetric and asymmetric rifting modes should result in partial break-up of the lithosphere, such as the break-up of the North Atlantic lithosphere. However, the current literature lacks effective ways to optimize tasks that are sensitive to boundary information, leading to subpar performances when applying these methods to detecting continuous shapes within images. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel boundary-sensitive information optimization method, incorporating an alternative form of contrastive loss function that concentrates on boundary-specific information contrast, thereby enhancing the efficiency of self-supervised segmentation. Moreover, we integrated a flexible sampling strategy along with a boundary-aware reconstruction loss function to enhance segmentation precision. Our method was thoroughly evaluated against leading self-supervised segmentation methods on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating notable improvements in segmentation accuracy, especially on datasets containing continuous shapes, with results matching or outperforming existing methods on other datasets. Furthermore, our method's effectiveness was also validated through a practical application in real-world medical imaging. Our optimized code is available for open review and modification. Our research identified potential areas for further research, specifically exploring ways to incorporate external annotated datasets and adapting the method for post-processing enhancements. With these potential extensions in mind, our results provide a solid foundation for the development of more sophisticated medical image segmentation protocols. Our study's success paves the way for exploring other transformation-based scenarios and loss function formulations as means to enhance self-supervised segmentation. With all modifications considered, our results serve as a prime example of the significant gains achievable through the refinement of initial protocol decisions. We introduce the G4C dataset, which enables the development of artificial intelligence responsible for guiding players in role-playing games through scenario-based storytelling. This collection of conversations is studied to reveal key elements of successful interactions, including the understanding of characters' mental states and the ability to predict others' thoughts and actions. In particular, our analysis highlights the importance of comprehending the intentions underlying other characters' actions, their perception of the game world, and the complexities of navigating multiple mental perspectives. Building upon this finding, we propose a proprietary dataset named LoRDS, which features Dungeon Master instructions derived from online resources, along with their associated mental state attributes. These annotations serve as a foundation for developing a leading model capable of engaging in conversations and guiding other characters through fantasy scenarios. This model's performance is assessed in a series of evaluations, including (1) Dungeon Master evaluation, where it is found to outperform alternative approaches by a significant margin (0.44 in NLU sub-score), (2) player evaluation, where it receives higher ratings than a baseline (3.73 out of 5) when given a choice between the model's instructions, and (3) mean average precision (MAP) evaluation, which shows an improvement of 0.11 when the model is given theory-of-mind information. This research contributes to the broader field of natural language instruction generation, particularly in scenarios involving interactive storytelling and multi-agent settings. The code for this study has been made available online at https://github.com/crafty-games-research/AIDM-HB. The datasets used in this research, namely the G4C dataset and LoRDS dataset, have also been made publicly available at https://github.com/crafty-games-research/G4C and https://github.com/crafty-games-research/LoRDS, respectively. These resources provide valuable groundwork for developing AI Dungeon Masters capable of creating engaging, meaningful experiences for players through scenario-based storytelling. The potential extensions to this research are also discussed in the conclusion. One potential extension involves the development of a player character that can grasp the Dungeon Master's mental state and adapt its actions accordingly, another potential extension involves the creation of a Dungeon Master that can anticipate a wide range of player actions, and another potential extension involves the creation of a more comprehensive theory-of-mind for multiple characters in the game. These potential extensions, along with the current research, contribute to the broader field of natural language instruction generation, particularly in scenarios involving interactive storytelling and multi-agent settings. To determine the significance of Early Dark Energy (EDE), we first compared the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS) models without EDE, then calculated the difference in their likelihood ratios. This methodology allowed us to quantify the evidence in favor of EDE given the current Planck and BOSS data, finding it equivalent to $2.3\sigma$ and significantly more compelling than similar models like vacuum energy. Furthermore, our approach identified a threshold on the EDE fraction at $\Omega_{\rm EDE}/\omega_{cdm} \approx 0.012$ below which the increase in likelihood cannot be distinguished from random fluctuation. Moreover, our method effectively constricted a recently proposed window on the EDE fraction, $\omega_{\rm EDE} / \omega_{s8} \approx 0.14$ at $0.018 < \omega_{s8} < 0.025$, as it holds within the broader range defined by the likelihood ratio at $0.015 < \omega_{s8} < 0.021$. Additionally, our approach found that the existing data already favor models with significant EDE over those without it at more than $4\sigma$ confidence when varying the number of neutrinos while keeping the total neutrino mass constant. Lastly, our methodology placed an upper limit on the EDE fraction at $\Omega_{\rm EDE}/\omega_{cdm} \approx 0.026$ when comparing the best-fit EDE model to the best-fit $\Lambda$CDM model, significantly more stringent than similar limits from other studies. Finally, our approach is highly versatile and can be applied to any existing or future cosmological data using the Bayes factors and profile likelihood methods. Additionally, we became aware of a study in progress by another research group which also explored the impact of EDE using the profile likelihood method for existing data, whereas our approach further develops this idea and accurately reflects the findings of the mentioned study. However, the mentioned study reported an incorrect figure of $1.5\sigma$ when comparing the likelihood ratio of the best-fit EDE model to the best-fit $\Lambda$CDM model, as the actual figure is significantly more compelling at $2.3\sigma$. Furthermore, DISCO demonstrates its practical applications by accurately identifying discriminatory language in real-world dialogues. The key advantage of our approach is its flexibility, allowing it to be adapted for various tasks while also being relatively easy to implement compared to other methods. These models perform poorly when confronted with complex phrases as input, which is evident from the low accuracy of counterfactuals generated for the ADVERSARIAL and WORDNET datasets. To move forward, it is essential to prioritize simplicity when designing the input phrases used for training these models. We have implemented this approach by dividing the PTA band into narrower segments and processing each segment individually using an accurate but computationally expensive method. This multi-scale strategy allows for a balance between the level of accuracy and computational expense by adjusting the size of the individual processing segments. Three-dimensional point cloud data can be generated from two-dimensional images by using techniques like lidar scanning or virtual reality synthesis.  Using this point cloud data, it's possible to estimate certain scene properties such as distance, angle, and even presence or absence of specific objects.  However, certain features like shadows pose a problem for these estimations as their appearance depends on various factors including how they're cast, the object that created them, and their location within the scene.  Since different techniques for analyzing these scenes treat shadows in distinct ways, it's necessary to account for the specific method being used.  To handle this complexity, a solution is proposed that defines a mapping between shadows and the scene's inherent properties, allowing for an optimization process to be implemented to regression models.  By doing so, the model can accurately predict shadow behavior on unseen data, even when the optimization process incites irregularities in the output, and the model can be modified to account for differences in various techniques, all while maintaining efficiency by using a solution that evaluates only a limited number of potential outcomes at a time.  This proposed solution is then applied to two types of cloud data generation methods, and the model's performance shows a notable gain, confirming the effectiveness of the shadow evaluation solution.  Since the solution involves differentiable code, it's also possible to integrate it with optimization methods that use backpropagation, allowing the model to be modified to output more accurate predictions of target images, which leads to even better results with the examples tested.  This proposed solution could potentially be useful in addressing other inverse problems by using a similar approach.  To facilitate further research, the code used for the experiments is made available on the official GitHub repository https://github.com/yutakotani93/diff_shadow, and the same repository contains additional details regarding the method's implementation, usage, and results. In this research, we develop a novel methodology to model uncertain variables, incorporating both unanticipated attacks and unreported successes. Our approach is based on an outcome-driven framework that connects program behavior to desired outcomes and probabilistically assesses program properties. We enhance this framework with our uncertainty modeling technique, which utilizes multivariate probability functions and utility theory. By integrating uncertain variables, the system becomes capable of selecting the most effective way to achieve desired outcomes with the available information. We apply this methodology to a case study involving a network of self-driving cars. Additionally, we create an interactive tool to assist human operators in understanding and adjusting the calibrated parameters of the system. Researchers have proposed several theories to explain these patterns using models such as gas supply and consumption, gas exchanges through interactions, and star formation efficiency (SFE) based on the presence or size of a bulge. At intermediate masses, typically above one billion solar masses, SFE reaches a maximum, explaining the turn-over in the M*-sSFR relation. The calculations yield an effective H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian with modified parameters that depend on the coefficients of the trial wavefunction. These parameters are determined to be in an unstable interval, consistent with empirical observations of the model. Additionally, we find that the system's total energy is expressible in a compact form involving the coefficients' squared values, providing further insight into the model's properties. Furthermore, we identify a critical value for the instability, which occurs at a specific value of the H\'enon-Heiles parameter. Parameters below this critical value are associated with bounded states of motion, while those above it are linked to chaotic conditions. The name "chaotic state" for this condition is justified by computations using the Jackiw-Kerman functional, which measure chaos levels and confirm that they reach a maximum when the system's wavefunction is orthogonal to its ground state. The findings with the Hatano-Sesevari trial wavefunction are compared to those from a similar approach with the H\'enon-Heiles trial wavefunction, which produces an identical results for energy and variance but different outcomes for the instability and chaos calculations. The reasons for these differences are analyzed in a comprehensive way. Lastly, we explore the connection between our implemented variational approach and the conventional method of minimizing total energy within the H\'enon-Heiles model. The results show that the conventional method overestimates the system's stability but still identifies the correct equilibrium points. Moreover, it distinguishes between regular and chaotic states, albeit not as precisely as the variational approach. The generalization of these findings to other types of trial wavefunctions that depend on parameters is also discussed. The conclusions emphasize that the value of these parameters, obtained through the minimalization of total energy within the context of the variational approach, provides accurate information about the system's behavior, even if they may not correspond to the actual parameter values of the underlying Hamiltonian. The name "effective parameter" is coined to describe these quantities. The theoretical framework presented can be applied to other multi-body systems by using the same variational approach. The proposed Hatano-Sesevari trial wavefunction can be modified to model dipole-dipole and Yukawa interactions. The concept of global simplicial bundles was introduced by Joyal and Zhenchang, building upon the ideas of Cisinski and Denisi, and it was proposed that the simplicial homotopy theory be based on global simplicial bundles rather than simplicial functors. In this paper, we examine a specific aspect of global simplicial bundles by demonstrating that they are equivalent to a specific type of simplicial category that is closely related to category theory. More specifically, we show that a global simplicial bundle can be represented as a simplicial category whose objects, morphisms, and higher morphisms are all equivalent to sets, and that this connection preserves the simplicial homotopy theory. Finally, we establish that using global simplicial bundles as simplicial functors results in a simplicial homotopy theory that is fully compatible with the original homotopy theory. Additionally, we introduce the concept of a global simplicial group, and demonstrate that it is the primary entity in the category of global simplicial sets over a simplicial category. Furthermore, we establish that global simplicial groups are the fundamental objects in the simplicial homotopy theory based on global simplicial bundles. Lastly, we demonstrate that this new homotopy theory is an abstract representation of the original homotopy theory. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of erroneous positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. This report outlines the development of a novel computing system, dubbed "Acropus," which integrates an addressable data array into a reconfigurable mesh of processors. Currently, this system is being implemented using a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). Acropus is designed to serve as a model for evaluating the performance of different algorithmic strategies, as its ease of programing is similar to that of a Central Processing Unit (CPU). Nevertheless, it offers a more detailed level of data structure interaction, comparable to that of a data-structured memory-based CPU. By utilizing a data addressable concurrent programming model, Acropus enables multiple data elements to be processed simultaneously, reducing the need for explicit synchronization instructions. This leads to a significant increase in the amount of usable memory bandwidth. To facilitate programing, a data addressable concurrent compiler is being developed in partnership with the University of Delaware, with a simple data flow graph-based programming language serving as the foundation. This programming language is easy to translate into the necessary configuration files required for the FPGA's programmable components. Our implementation of the data addressable concurrent processor uses configuration bits known as Distributed Memory Interfaces, which provide a memory interface similar to that of a CPU memory map. This has the benefit of enhancing system flexibility by allowing different algorithmic techniques to be easily integrated into Acropus. Our data addressable concurrent processor has been put through its paces using a variety of benchmark tests, including matrix multiplication, BINARY SEARCH, INSERTION SORT, and a custom image processing application. These tests have demonstrated significant performance gains resulting from the utilization of multiple data elements, with further improvement potential being held up by the limitations of the FPGA technology used. With regard to programming complexity, Acropus offers a level of abstraction comparable to that of a CPU, while simultaneously providing a level of data structure interaction that is comparable to that of a data-structured memory-based CPU. This is accomplished through the use of a single instruction that combines a memory address and an operation, a feature that is currently the subject of U.S. Patent No. 10,246,821. This level of abstraction, combined with the data addressable concurrent programming model, results in highly efficient performance, as evidenced by the matrix multiplication example, which achieves a throughput of over 1 teraflop on the Xilinx Kintex A2000 FPGA. This report provides a technical overview of the data addressable concurrent processor project, with further development details being available through public source code repositories. Recent breakthroughs in neural-based code generation have highlighted the potential of combining neural networks with symbolic computation for superior results.  Despite achieving high accuracy in specific tasks, the underlying code produced by these models often lacks the clarity of true code, which is rectified by the proposed method of using the symbols for static evaluation within the neural network.  By incorporating a separate symbolic representation of the code, the neural network can generate more readable and functional code, as evidenced by the improved outcomes of the method when evaluated by human assessors and automated tools for code quality.  The method also facilitates the identification of errors in the code by leveraging the separate symbolic code, which results in a 25% reduction in code that requires rewriting due to the introduction of errors during generation.  The proposed system achieves these results using a combination of a transformer-based neural network and a technique for symbolic manipulation of the code, specifically tree transformation, which is applicable across various programming languages despite their differences in syntax and semantics.  The method and the associated dataset are made publicly available to facilitate further research in neural-based code generation, which is accompanied by the results of a user study conducted with independent code developers.  The outcomes reveal that the generated code not only meets the expectations of human assessors in terms of functionality and readability but also complements the code generated using traditional template-based methods, which is reflected in the improved outcome when the method is combined with the baseline approach.  The study also sheds light on the variables that influence the performance of the system, which is characterized by a long-tail distribution of the generated code, with most successful outcomes resulting from the generation of simple methods.  The analysis of the code and the associated evaluation functions, which is facilitated by the separation of the symbolic code, reveals that the system excels in producing code with optimal performance, which is achieved in 20% of the cases, and also accelerates the development of efficient code by reducing the time spent on each function by a factor of three.  The associated code and models are available at https://github.com/amir-archi/neuralfp-code-gen.  This work is a extension of our previous research on the application of pre-trained neural models in code search and generation, which was presented at the ICLR 2021 workshop on Machine Learning for Code.  The study has been recognized as one of the top submissions at the CodeML 2021 workshop and has been cited in multiple code-related research papers presented at conferences and forums such as NIPS, ICLR, ICML

A crucial attribute of encryption is the coherence between privacy and security guarantees. It ensures that learning someone's plaintext does not reveal their original encrypted message, whereas the same is true for learning their encrypted data does not reveal their plaintext. This underlying principle applies to user-independent decryption, the type employed in contemporary homomorphic encryption systems. Although widely adopted, there is a lack of research into user-dependent decryption that can withstand state coercion. This study fills this gap by designing a new, technically straightforward decryption procedure that can resist the coercion of an all-powerful state even when facing an infinite number of queries from an infinite number of users. This new construction can serve as the foundation for creating novel CoERC protocols. As an example of this protocol's utility, we propose a new election system, called El-Gamal-Election, which ensures secrecy and integrity for elections conducted with encrypted ballots. Our experimentally verified implementation shows that these new CoERC protocols can run at a practical speed for large-scale elections. Furthermore, we introduce a new definition called'decryption integrity' that can be applied to any encryption framework. This definition enables us to prove the security of our new user-dependent decryption procedure in the standard model, which provides better theoretical guarantees than our existing implementation. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of creating election systems with specific features and the results of our experiments provide valuable insights for future research. This study's innovative contribution can also benefit other CoERC protocol research. In particular, we propose a new method for combining multiple encryption frameworks, referred to as 'fusion,' which could lead to the development of more secure election systems in the future. In recent years, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have reached superior levels in various classification tasks, largely due to their massive computational resources and vast amounts of training data available. Despite their impressive performance, the underlying mechanics of DNNs remain unclear, with concerns being raised about their reliability and potential lack of transparency. This study aims to address these issues by thoroughly examining the internal workings of DNNs. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of multiple convolutional neural network architectures, including their parameter distributions, feature extraction processes, and error propagation patterns. Our findings reveal interesting insights into the internal dynamics of DNNs, including the unique capabilities of each architecture in processing visual information and the limitations of non-linear hidden layers in understanding this data. These discoveries could have significant implications for the selection of network architectures for computer vision applications. We also developed a straightforward method to visualize the cumulative effects of error propagation within DNNs, which could be useful for identifying potential limitations of these networks. This study provides valuable knowledge that can be applied to enhance the performance, as well as the comprehensibility and reliability, of DNNs. We believe these contributions will be particularly useful for researchers working in the field of computer vision. To improve this, we propose a cutting-edge model that utilizes a progressive approach to generate high-resolution, nuanced lesions. By combining a Variational Auto-Encoder with the help of a discriminative model, we incorporate both the global characteristics and local features of lesions into our predictions. By progressively adding layer details during training, our model is able to produce more precise predictions in higher resolution images. The concept of quantum nonlocality, initially found in entangled states, can also occur in unextendible product bases (UPBs) - a phenomenon studied in the field of unextendible product frameworks. UPBs comprise multiple product states that cannot be created with a pure product state. In this study, we examine the quantum nonlocality within UPBs in a variety of systems, from spin systems to continuous-mode optical systems. To accomplish this, we developed a novel method for identifying the most robust states within a given UPB by measuring the reduction in entropy when a system interacts with its corresponding UPB. This measure serves as an indicator for the quantum nonlocality present in each system. Utilizing this approach, we found that the largest reduction in entropy among UPB states consistently correlates with the smallest number of systems required to represent those states. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this relationship can result in categories of systems that are or are not capable of supporting robust quantum nonlocality. Additionally, we introduced the concept of semi-extended product channels, which allows us to explore the spread of quantum nonlocality throughout systems of different dimensions. Our findings indicate that the unique spectral characteristics of a system's channel can influence its ability to support robust quantum nonlocality. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of robust quantum nonlocality in heterogeneous systems, which may have implications for the development of secure quantum communication protocols that can accommodate various technological setups. Moreover, our findings reveal that continuous-mode optical systems possess robust quantum nonlocality in a broader range of situations than spin systems, which may make them better suited for applications requiring the implementation of quantum nonlocality. Utilizing our proposed framework, researchers can explore a wide range of topics in the field of unextendible product frameworks, such as resolving long-standing issues in spin systems and examining the relationship between UPBs and quantum error correction codes in continuous-mode optical systems. Our study exposes several hypothetical scenarios for detecting robust quantum nonlocality, which could be applied to investigate the presence of this phenomenon in more complex systems. Additionally, our results can be experimentally verified through spectral analysis of the reduced states produced by interacting systems with their corresponding UPBs. Our study expands the theoretical understanding of unextendible product frameworks by introducing novel strategies for identifying quantum nonlocality within these frameworks, which may have implications for the development of secure quantum communication protocols that can accommodate various technological setups. Working with categorical data in models that select a subset of variables poses significant challenges due to the issues of categorical data scaling and feature interdependence. Despite these difficulties, the Group Lasso method remains an important tool for model reduction. To overcome these limitations and expand the scalability of Group Lasso to include interactions within categories, we develop two innovations. Firstly, we present a new sparse model that incorporates a scaling technique for categorical data and a robust information criterion. Secondly, we propose a fitting algorithm that participates in the Bregman distance algorithm and achieves consistent parameter estimation. Moreover, this proposed method surpasses the traditional Group Lasso in both prediction accuracy and model size. Additionally, we explore the computational efficiency of this algorithm, demonstrating its applicable scaling to high-dimensional data through a series of theoretical scalability tests. Furthermore, we conduct a comparative analysis of our method's performance against state-of-the-art techniques such as Group Lasso and Lasso on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which reveals our method's superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model sparsity. Despite its efficient computation, our method still faces challenges in handling extremely large datasets due to the requirement for an efficient inner optimization solution. To address this limitation, we explore further the potential of batch optimization methods such as Block Coordinate Descent, which is currently under investigation. Nonetheless, our proposed model offers a ground-breaking framework for developing high-dimensional modeling that captures complex interactions within nominal data by scaling and participating in an information criterion. This model provides a robust framework for developing new algorithms that can handle sparse, linear models in high-dimensional data scenarios. This work is an extension of our previous research on group feature selection methods. We believe that our proposed model has the potential to address challenging data scaling and interdependence issues common in big data scenarios. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Next steps will involve a comparative analysis of our data with other observations of our targets to derive a more comprehensive understanding, in addition to expanding our study to a broader range of galaxy mergers. Additionally, we will utilize our data to model the velocity and spatial distributions of the ionized gas in our targets. Furthermore, our study will serve as a foundation for studying the evolution of galaxy mergers through the detection of gas outflows, a process that has the potential to be influenced by active supermassive black holes. Moreover, we will investigate the link between gas outflows and the growth of supermassive black holes, a process that is likely powered by active galactic nuclei. Lastly, our study will enable us to examine the role of active supermassive black holes in shaping the spatial and velocity distributions of the ionized gas in galaxy mergers. Ultimately, our study will contribute to a broader understanding of the relationship between active supermassive black holes and the physical properties of galaxy mergers. The multivariate interpolation operator is a fundamental concept used in both scattered data interpolation and surface reconstruction methods like Subdivision Surface rendering. While piecewise linear interpolation operators are widely employed for this purpose, they introduce unwanted angles at interpolation points, thus degrading the accuracy of interpolations, especially in smooth surface representations. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel set of linear combinations for standard cubic splines that maintain consistency with the original data set at interpolation points, allowing for precise preservation of angle and curve orientation. Building on this innovation, this paper develops a form-preserving quasi-interpolation operator using a new family of transcendental radial basis functions, which meets the consistency conditions at interpolation points without resorting to local reconstruction of interpolation spaces. This unorthodox approach enables the construction of smooth surfaces from scattered data points, preserving their original orientation, making it particularly suitable for rendering and other applications requiring surface smoothness. Moreover, this paper investigates the convergence properties of this new quasi-interpolation operator, proving that it shares the same order of convergence as traditional linear quasi-interpolation operators. The development and performance of this innovative operator are illustrated through examples, including a visualization application, and its source code is made freely available for download. Additionally, this paper introduces a new radial basis function formulation for solving linear systems efficiently, which could be of independent interest for solving other types of radial basis function-based problems. The convergence analysis of the new quasi-interpolation operator is supported by an error bound, which is an advancement over previous related work. Specifically, the new error bound improves the previous best known result by several terms, which is verified numerically for a range of data sets. The formulation of the new radial basis function involves a novel determination of the free parameter through the intersection point of two curves, which is an innovative feature that enables local support of the operator. This property, along with the preservation of angle and curve orientation, enables the construction of smooth surfaces from scattered data points, which has been successfully applied in visualization and reconstruction problems. The development of the new quasi-interpolation operator is an independent outcome of the authors' previous related work, which explored global formulation and local reconstruction methods in combination. The novel radial basis function and its performance have been independently verified by an independent researcher. By successfully completing this task, it's possible to create interactive 360-degree videos using the original audio and a selected viewport. To accomplish this, we've developed a framework that incorporates a viewer model, which is broken down into two components: a viewport model and a caption model. The viewport model is trained using a dataset composed of labeled viewport segments, while the caption model is trained separately to analyze the relationship between captions and viewports. Once the viewer model is trained, it can be used to generate high-quality viewport predictions for new, unseen data. Our experimental analysis includes a thorough evaluation of various approach variations and verification of the significance of viewer modeling. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. This strategy, however, raises questions about the inherent statistical significance of the found results. Omitting glitch-affected data may not entirely eliminate potential weaknesses, as it only addresses observable fluctuations and doesn't account for those that could go undetected. It is essential to recognize that in the search for such rare events, there is inevitably a limit to how much data can be usefully analyzed before false positives become more likely. This limitation is particularly noticeable in the experiment's current data, where the ratio of detected glitches to undetected ones is influenced by the time it takes to cross the satellite's protective layer. Despite this, by comparing this time to the orbital and spinning cycles, the overall data exclusion policy still holds. A more detailed analysis of the data with the current criteria of excluding data from periods with detected glitches reveals that this rule is followed for about 99% of the total available data. Furthermore, the consequences of incorporating data from glitch events are expressed in terms of the allowable variation in the gravitational constant. This, in turn, raises the bar for future experiments aiming to surpass the Microscope test's sensitivity.
