In transfer learning, a model utilizes previous experience to achieve high accuracy on new tasks. One prominent approach is known as zero-shot learning, which enables a model to accurately classify unfamiliar data types (classes) without being trained on those specific types. One area where models are commonly trained on data with known labels is computer vision, where they are often tasked with identifying various objects or performing certain actions on images. One method to achieve zero-shot learning in vision involves using a technique called prompt-based visual language that allows a model to utilize natural language to define the tasks. However, this approach relies on the presence of relevant data with labels, which is often impractical or impossible to obtain when adapting the model to new, unseen data types (classes). In contrast, a different approach involves using a model that can make decisions on classification tasks without revealing the underlying reasoning, which is known as a black-box framework. In this study, we propose a new zero-shot knowledge transfer framework that utilizes decision-based black-box models, where the models can make decisions on classification tasks without sharing their internal workings. This proposed framework includes a zero-shot classification module that uses a prompt-based visual language model to accurately identify data types (classes) based on decisions made by the black-box models. This enables the model to accurately classify various data types (classes) without being trained on data with corresponding labels, which is especially useful when labels are expensive to obtain or cannot be obtained at all. This proposed framework also includes a data selection module that selects the most relevant data examples for the new data types (classes) by analyzing decisions made by the black-box models, which in turn enables the model to accurately classify more data examples on the new data types (classes) without being trained on data with corresponding labels. Throughout their operational life, radio detectors like CHORDA in PAO system experience beam-induced fluctuations causing short-term variations in the reading of background levels. This phenomenon necessitates frequent monitoring of the detector's performance through scanning its electronic chain. This scanning process involves activating the detector's gain to maximum capacity and collecting data at a fixed rate as a sweeping beam scans the sky. Subsequent analysis of this data involves calculating the typical features of beam-induced fluctuations to ensure the detector is performing within desired standards. If necessary, further adjustments to the detector's settings can be made to restore optimal performance. This process demands a detailed understanding of beam-induced fluctuations to differentiate them from background levels, which could be influenced by solar wind, cosmic rays, or the Earth's magnetic field. Several key indicators of these fluctuations have been established as benchmarks by previous analysis of data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. If these indicators fall within specified ranges, it indicates the detector is performing as expected during that particular scan. If the conditions are not met, the data generated may need to undergo additional processing to mitigate beam-induced fluctuations before it can be utilized in statistical analyses of the data. This process involves employing specialized software to filter out data that does not meet the required standards. If necessary, further adjustments to the detector's settings can be made to restore optimal performance. In this project, we propose developing a dedicated database to house the detection settings, associated analysis software, and relevant beam-induced fluctuation data. This database will serve as a resource for researchers involved in this project, while also providing a foundation for extending this approach to other radio detectors used in point-source optical system systems. Furthermore, we will explore integrating a feature that generates customized scanning protocols tailored to the unique requirements of different detectors and their operational settings. This will involve collaborating with the manufacturer of these detectors to obtain detailed information on their internal components, along with a discussion on the need for developing a formal protocol for this process. If accepted, this project will be presented at the 37th International Symposium on Astrophysics and Space Science held in Bali, Indonesia from the 21st to the 25th of September, 2020. In connection with this project, we will also be submitting a separate paper titled "Analysis of Background Data from CHORDA during PAO Beam Scans" to the same conference. That paper will provide a more in-depth examination of the background data collected during the beam scanning process, with a focus on verifying whether the features of beam-induced fluctuations in radio detectors match those predicted by theoretical models.

Its binary erasure channel (BEC) performance is examined when the source and decoder communicate independently. A unique construction method for regular DDR LDPC codes is also presented, and a particular code ensemble that combines opposing degree distributions is shown to achieve optimal performance on the BEC. The proposed code's performance is compared to that of conventional repeat-accumulate (RA) codes and a new "double-RA" code ensemble is defined. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the inner workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the difficulty of distinguishing a pyramid scheme from other multi-level marketing businesses. Due to the intricate design of Forsage, with features such as refund pools and investment minimums, it is difficult to identify the scam's underlying pyramid structure. Our study is relevant to research on hidden financial transactions, intelligent contracts, blockchain technology, and the economics of digital technology. It showcases the potential of transparent data to analyze the empirical effects of smart-contract-based schemes and may serve as a model for investigating other visible blockchain transactions. By combining automated data analysis with expert review of code and content, our study shows the value of interdisciplinary research on the intersection of technology and economics. This type of research can provide valuable insights on the impact of digital technology on economic transactions and is a crucial component of a framework for responsible innovation in this domain. This framework is outlined in an appendix to this article. It encompasses guidelines for developers of digital technology, due diligence procedures for investors, and best practices for users of digital technology. This framework can be applied to a broad range of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, internet of things devices, and decentralized autonomous systems. It is particularly relevant to developing countries with limited regulatory frameworks, where the speed and security of blockchain transactions can create an environment conducive to the proliferation of hidden financial transactions and other malicious activities enabled by digital technology. This framework can also serve as a model for addressing the technological aspects of economic transactions in other contexts where technology and economics intersect. This is exemplified by the issue of gas prices in blockchain transactions, which can be viewed as pricing for computer processing power

The Generative Adversarial Network has been the leading text generation model in recent years due to its potential for improving language understanding and production. Despite this, the fully connected nature of traditional GANs leads to difficulties in achieving a balance between training and implementing a sparse attention mechanism. This study introduces a novel independent situational awareness approach for swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles. The proposed method allows each UAV to independently analyze its surroundings using a localized coordinate system based on its neighbors' position data. This enables the UAVs to identify and track targets, as well as navigate through obstacle-detecting capabilities. To test this method, a simulated swarm environment was created, and the results showed that the proposed system can accurately determine target positions, positioning, and approach distances. Furthermore, the independent situational awareness approach allows for more resilient swarm performance, as the removal of a single UAV does not disrupt the entire swarm's understanding of its environment. Overall, this approach offers a robust and reliable solution for swarms to interact with their surroundings autonomously. To demonstrate the practical applications of this technology, the approach was integrated with a sample controller, resulting in the successful execution of target tracking and surround navigation tasks. This independent situational awareness approach can also be adapted for other types of swarms operating in different environments. To facilitate this, we developed a general framework that can be applied across various swarm contexts. This independent situational awareness approach can be applied to unmanned ground vehicles as well, and we are currently exploring its potential extension to unmanned surface vehicles. This research can be expanded to address more complex targets, such as those in cluttered environments or with unknown shapes, which would enable the proposed system to effectively detect and track these more complex targets as well. Additionally, we are investigating ways to enhance the reliability of this approach by incorporating redundant target position sensors in the swarm. This could be achieved through the use of sensor arrays or multiple UAVs with position sensors, and we are exploring ways to integrate this redundancy effectively. This could potentially allow the system to recover from the loss of a single UAV's position sensor, and we are currently developing methods for triggering this recovery process. This research is being advanced as part of the AFWERX Phase 2 SBIR program, and we are collaborating with multiple industry and academic partners to accelerate the development of this technology. This includes a strong focus on accelerating the transition of this innovation from the laboratory to operational military settings. As part of this effort, we are currently working with the Air Force to establish a rigorous testing and validation process for this technology, and we are exploring ways to integrate this approach with real-world military communications and navigation systems. To study these phenomena, researchers need reliable methods to quantify polarization within social structures. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) utilizing both learned representations and ranking objectives; and 2) resolving the gap between the single-model optimizer and multi-teacher distillation process. To tackle these issues, we combine the representations from multiple teachers through a pairwise iterative aggregation method, incorporating both the learned representations and ranking losses from each teacher. Then, we apply a weighted average procedure to obtain a final aggregated distribution from all teachers. This aggregated distribution is used as the target distribution for the student model during the optimization process. Our proposed method achieves a notable 12% improvement in NDCG and 15% improvement in DCG over the baseline model, ultimately resulting in a student model with performance comparable to the teacher model. Moreover, our method achieves this performance using only half the number of optimization iterations required for a baseline model, indicating a practical application for this method in real-world ranking systems. This weakness is illustrated using a 2D Ising model with competing interactions, where an initial stoquastic Hamiltonian gradually becomes anti-fermionic and non-stoquastic. Despite the presence of decoherence, which breaks quantum coherence, we find that quantum annealing fails due to a catastrophic collapse of overlap for sufficiently large antiferromagnetic strengths. This failure cannot be anticipated classically, where a critical point is found at which the structure of local minima changes, potentially protecting quantum annealing from failure. Notably, this protection can be achieved by introducing artificial decoherence in the form of a transverse magnetic field, which facilitates quantum annealing even without actual decoherence. These findings suggest that quantum annealing should involve a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian to ensure effectiveness and highlight the crucial role of decoherence in this process. Finally, applications to the optimization of Ising models on random graph structures are also considered, showing that quantum annealing can be more efficient than classical methods like the weighted majority vote. Additionally, introducing artificial decoherence in certain samples is found to further increase the efficacy of quantum annealing, suggesting that this technique holds significant potential for solving complex optimization problems efficiently. This essay explores the life and work of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, a distinguished Dutch astronomer, through his role at Kapteyn's Astronomical Observatory. Van Rhijn succeeded Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn as director in 1911 and went on to become a leading figure in international astronomy, serving as president of the International Astronomical Union. During his tenure, he oversaw the completion of the Henry Draper Catalogue and initiated the Cordoba Southern Sky Catalogue. His contributions also included developing the scheme for selected areas, which would be continued by the Palomar Sky Survey, a legacy that cemented his influence on 20th-century astronomy. Van Rhijn's career and achievements reflect his dedication to his mentor's legacy and his own visionary approach to astronomical research. His life came full circle with a fitting tribute when the name Van Rhijn was assigned to a feature in the Geminid meteor stream, a recognition of his own significant contributions to the field. Van Rhijn passed away in 1973 at the age of 87, his legacy enduring as a testament to his extraordinary life's work. His autobiography, published in 1946, provides a detailed account of his life and career, a personal narrative that offers valuable insights into the development of astronomy during the 20th century. This essay is an extension of that autobiography, shedding new light on van Rhijn's life and work in the latter period of his life and career. It brings together new information and a more nuanced analysis to further illuminate his life and legacy. It is my pleasure to present this essay as a tribute to van Rhijn's life and work, a gesture of appreciation for the significant role he played in the history of astronomy. It is also my intention to make this essay available to the International Astronomical Union in consideration of their decision to designate Van Rhijn as one of the heroes of astronomy. This decision was influential in inspiring me to explore van Rhijn's life and work in greater detail, a topic that I am proud to have had the opportunity to study and present publicly. As the size of neural networks continues to grow, model-parallel learning has become a key technique for training these complex networks on multiple GPUs. However, an equally pressing challenge remains: efficiently training a large number of models. To address this, we propose a novel approach called Regional Reviewer Training, which builds on the reviewer-encoder framework by limiting the exchange of information between models to a partial update. By doing so, we significantly reduce the overhead of inter-GPU communication. Furthermore, we introduce a simple convolutional encoder that simplifies data sharing and reduces the computational burden. We showcase the effectiveness of Regional Reviewer Training across various deep neural networks and datasets, showcasing its robust performance and a notable improvement in training time. For instance, on the ImageNet dataset, Regional Reviewer Training achieves a remarkable 2x speedup over the standard model-parallel learning approach using six GPUs. The code for Regional Reviewer Training is publicly available on GitHub. As the field of model-parallel learning continues to evolve, we anticipate our approach will serve as a key building block for future efficient deep neural network training methods. Additionally, we contribute a comprehensive benchmark that facilitates the evaluation of model-parallel learning methods, encompassing a diverse range of deep neural networks and datasets spanning the Object Recognition, Segmentation, and Classification domains. This benchmark, dubbed ParLearn-Bench, offers a crucial resource for assessing the performance, efficiency, and practicality of model-parallel learning approaches. With the ongoing growth of neural networks, our work underscores the importance of optimizing model-parallel learning for both efficiency and accuracy, a challenge that will only intensify in the future. Nonetheless, we believe that the field of model-parallel learning remains vibrant and full of opportunities for innovation and discovery. In particular, we expect the development of new neural network architectures that embrace parallelism by design, along with increased access to high-performance hardware designed specifically for model-parallel learning, will continue to shape the trajectory of the field. As such, we anticipate that future deep neural network training will heavily rely on model-parallel learning approaches, fueled by the escalating computational demands of big-GPU training. Despite the progress made in recent years, the field of model-parallel learning remains in its relative infancy, with much work still to be done in order to fully unlock the performance potential of high-performance hardware. Nonetheless, we are confident that the field will continue to evolve and shape the future of deep neural network training. Building upon this theory, we propose a mathematical model utilizing a graph theorem to predict an atom's electrical properties based on its electronic structure. This model demonstrates the value of complexity in atoms' electronic configurations and may provide a foundation for further insights into the properties of matter. The model's applicability is examined through a framework of simplicity, and we explore the possibility of extending this approach to address additional questions in chemistry. Furthermore, we discuss potential ways to implement this model using a computer program. The proposed model may be a useful tool for teaching the relationships between atoms' electronic structures and their properties. The name "LESS" is suggested as a label for this model, and we explore the connection between this model and the concept of simplicity known from cluster expansion. This study investigates the impact of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track with course material during the pandemic. We distinguish between two types of students: those who are self-motivated and those who are externally motivated. Our hypothesis is that remote learning has a positive effect on externally motivated students but a negative effect on self-motivated students. To support this hypothesis, we gather data from a survey conducted by the online learning platform, where users provided information about their motivation for learning online. We based our measurement of staying on course with learning metrics from online activity, specifically the average number of days spent learning each week. We identified key indicators, including age, motivation source, number of children, and employment status, that influence a student's ability to stay on course. We used these indicators to group students into three categories: young externally motivated students, middle-aged self-motivated students, and older externally motivated students. We based our analysis on a dataset of 1,000 users who learned online during the pandemic, relying on a method called clustering analysis to identify these student groups. The results of our study confirm our initial hypothesis, showing that remote learning had a positive effect on young externally motivated students and a negative effect on middle-aged self-motivated students. It's worth noting that online learning during the pandemic was quite different from traditional classroom settings, lacking the social aspect that is crucial for self-motivated students. Additionally, there were unexpected findings from our study, particularly the observation that young externally motivated students experienced a significant increase in online learning time, while middle-aged self-motivated students saw a notable decrease. On the other hand, older externally motivated students surprisingly spent less time learning online than they did before the pandemic. We offered a theory to explain these outcomes, referring to the life cycle model of learning, which posits that externally motivated students in both their young and older stages tend to learn online more efficiently, while self-motivated students in the middle stage of their life require more internal motivation to learn online. We also found that remote learning had a significant impact on older externally motivated students who spent less time learning online than they did before the pandemic, likely due to decreased online learning skills over time. Our study provides valuable insights for educators and online learning platform designers to create more effective online courses that cater to various student motivations, as well as strategies for retaining students' capability to stay on course with course material. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of considering life cycle factors when designing online learning programs, especially during times of significant change

For Toda conformal field theories based on simple Lie algebras, spinless vertex operators that satisfy Ward identities can be used to create primary fields from a Casimir function related to the algebras' root system. In this paper, we provide specific examples of these primary fields for the Toda model based on the A_2 algebra, specifically for the fundamental series with central charge $c > 2$. We derive a set of independent Casimir functions that can be used to describe all spinless primary fields, and verify that the associated vertex operators obey the given Ward identities. These identities allow us to define a conserved current in the model, and we determine the largest operator that can be created by this current. Additionally, we examine the operator product of two primary fields created by two different conserved currents, and find that the result contains a singular part that can be expressed as a sum over the squares of the algebra's root system. This particular outcome arises solely in the A_2 Toda theory among the conformal field theories based on simple Lie algebras. Furthermore, we establish that the critical exponents of the model can be obtained through a conformally invariant flow that connects it to a critical point defined by a set of primary fields, all of which create conformally invariant states. This interpretation leads to a demonstration that the central charge of the model can be determined by a universal quantity that is independent of the specific state. This result is also expressed in terms of the algebra's root system, and therefore holds a physical significance related to the model's conservation laws. This approach can be applied across all Toda conformal field theories based on simple Lie algebras, providing an overall framework that incorporates spinless vertex operators and related conservation laws. This framework is particularly useful in defining primary fields and verifying the associated Ward identities, which in turn enable the determination of the model's central charge and a set of independent Casimir functions that can create all spinless primary fields. This knowledge is crucial in identifying the largest operator that can be generated by a conserved current, as well as the operator product of two primary fields, which produces a singular part that can be expressed as a sum over the algebra's root system. This framework will be integral in our future research, where we plan to further examine the models' critical exponents and determine the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian for the model's ground state and all higher excitation levels. This will involve specifying the primary fields that create these states, as well as identifying all primary fields

Investigating the thermodynamics and feeble cosmic censorship conjecture of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes requires analyzing their behavior when a scalar field is added. This paper examines the impact of this scalar field on both thermodynamic stability and feeble cosmic censorship, particularly in relation to minimum and maximum values of the scalar field. It also discusses the implications of these constraints on temperature and the scalar field's potential to violate the cosmic censorship policy. Results show that when the scalar field's energy is less than half of the black hole's charge, it cannot cause instability or violate the cosmic censorship conjecture. Additionally, in cases where the scalar field's energy equals half of the charge, stability is determined by specific conditions related to both thermodynamics and the feeble cosmic censorship conjecture. Conversely, if the scalar field's energy exceeds half of the charge, the system inevitably experiences thermodynamic instability. It is also found that the feeble cosmic censorship conjecture is always valid when the scalar field's energy is greater than half of the charge. It is worth noting that in situations where the scalar field's energy is exactly half of the charge, the system experiences borderline thermodynamic stability. It is also determined that this midpoint represents a nonlinear accumulation point for all potential trajectories. It is interesting to observe that this behavior is analogous to that described by the curve shortening equation, which is a well-documented phenomenon in geometric evolution equations. It is also determined that the specific conditions that allow for instability or a violation of the cosmic censorship conjecture occur precisely where the scalar field's energy is marginally sufficient to cause instability. It is worth noting that in cases where the scalar Field's energy is significantly greater than half of the charge, the system's behavior becomes so unstable that it provides little insight into the cosmic censorship conjecture. It is also determined that in cases where the scalar field's energy is less than half of the charge, as well as in situations where the scalar field's energy is greater than twice the charge, the minimum value of the scalar field is determined by specific conditions related to thermodynamics, while the maximum value of the scalar field is determined by specific conditions related to the feeble cosmic censorship conjecture. It is also determined that in cases where the scalar field's energy is exactly half of the charge, or exactly twice the charge, the minimum value of the scalar field is determined by specific conditions related to thermodynamics, while the maximum value of the scalar field is determined by specific conditions related to the feeble cosmic censorship conjecture

Humans walk by alternately activating their left and right legs through a complex central control system. Using a quantum circuit model with a specific quantum error syndrome correction code, we developed a coder that used reinforcement learning to optimize its performance, resulting in a significant improvement (a factor of at least 20) over conventional methods in simulations of actual quantum processing units. The code for this coder can be adapted to handle various coding scenarios. Furthermore, an open-source framework that integrates coder code and facilitates easier coder development has been released on GitHub, making it simpler to experiment with different coding techniques. With the option for hosting on Google Cloud, this framework can be used to train coders on a broader range of quantum error syndromes. The development of this coder and framework has paved the way for the exploration of more complex encoded qubit applications, such as the fabrication of fault-tolerant quantum gates and the execution of quantum circuits, with optimized coding, as well as the integration of coder performance into overall quantum processing unit performance metrics. The name of this coding method is Coderelearn, which stands for the combination of coder and reinforcement learning. The Coderelearn approach can also be applied to other quantum computing architectures, such as continuous variable quantum computing, solid-state qubits, and superconducting qubits, and has been successfully tested on actual processing units, resulting in improved performance. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome in terms of precision, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with complex systems that require significant manipulation of states. An alternative approach, known as quantum leap metrology, bypasses the need for such manipulation by using quantum transitions between states that are directly connected, which facilitates the measurement of multiple unknown angles simultaneously. This paper demonstrates the capabilities of this approach by showing that, in a system consisting of two interconnected cavities and utilizing laser light, it is possible to achieve the same level of precision improvement characteristic of quantum-dominated measurements. Furthermore, this approach exhibits greater robustness to decoherence and temperature-related fluctuations, as evidenced by optical double-resonance experiments conducted in a dual-cavity setup. The outcomes agree with theoretical simulations and indicate that this type of metrology can provide the most precise outcomes when certain conditions are met, such as reaching a certain level of coupling between cavities and optimizing the intensity of an external laser source. The findings also imply that quantum leap metrology could serve as a practical means of achieving the greatest possible precision in the measurement of physical parameters, without having to engage in complicated quantum state manipulations. This paper concludes by outlining potential applications and future experimentation opportunities with quantum leap metrology, particularly in dual-cavity setups using laser light, as well as the prospect of applying this approach to more complex systems and using a variety of different types of radiation. Furthermore, it explores the possibility of combining quantum leap metrology with other approaches to further improve the precision of measurements, especially when dealing with complex systems that are difficult to manipulate using other methods. This paper investigates the extreme gains achieved by optimally regulating power in interference networks with any power level, as opposed to binary power control. We demonstrate that the optimally regulated power's extreme gains rise at a rate of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ in $K$-user interference networks, indicating that this benefit becomes significantly larger as the number of users increases. Furthermore, we show that this scaling relationship applies across a broad spectrum of scenarios, including those with either positive or negative external interference, as well as those with either the ability or the inability to selectively eliminate interfering links. We argue that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ scaling relationship represents the fundamental extremal property of power regulation in general interference networks. Finally, we examine whether this $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ scaling relationship holds if the binary power control technique is replaced by another form of discrete power control. We find that the newly derived bounds converge to the previously established $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ limits as the discrete power control's step size increases, indicating that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit continues to rise with the number of users even with this alternative strategy. We derive a specific, precisely quantifiable extremal gain of approximately $K^{0.5}$ for four-user networks, serving as a cornerstone for further analysis of higher-user networks. Furthermore, we investigate whether this $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit is unique to power regulation, or if it applies broadly to other capacity-achieving strategies, such as those involving the signal-to-leakage ratio or the effective noise resistance. We also explore the relationship between this $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit and other measures of extremal gain, including those involving the harmonic mean and the minimum value. Finally, we investigate the extremal gains achieved by optimized strategies in multi-user networks. We find that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit continues to rise with the number of users even in such scenarios, and that this benefit increases at a rate of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ in $K$-user interference networks. We also examine the impact of other external interference on these optimized strategies, and derive a set of optimized bounds that converge to the previously established $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ limits as the external interference decreases. We then investigate the extremal gains achieved by optimized strategies in networks with external interference, and find that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit continues to rise with the number of users even in such scenarios.

A key challenge for legged robots navigating diverse terrain is the transition from rigid to deformable ground. In this research, we focus on a single robotic foot hopping over deformable surface using a simplified model. The model is based on an approach where surface impact is reclassified as a continuous process of increasing stiffness, simulating a foot that gradually sinks into the surface. The model is used to explore the conditions necessary for the robotic foot to execute successful hopping movements. Additionally, we develop a mathematical method to calculate an optimal amount of energy for initializing the robotic foot's hopping movement on soft ground. This model is applied to simulate the behavior of a single robotic foot on soft ground using simulation and physical testing. As a extension of this research, we experiment with enhancing the robotic foot's ability to hop on soft ground by introducing a spring-based system within the foot itself. The results of this research could provide a foundation for developing more complex robotic systems capable of navigating diverse terrain. The models and methods explored in this research are also presented in the associated video and code available online. The method for simulating and modeling the robotic foot's behavior on soft ground could potentially be adapted for applications involving surface interaction in fluid environments. We employ a contact interaction model, where the complexity of meson structure is accounted for by an external field, to consistently explain the volume independence of vacuum meson properties. This approach is utilized to compute the elastic shape factors of mesons within a quark-gluon plasma at finite temperature and chemical potential. Our analysis leverages a contact interaction model that is applicable to both the light mesons (pi, K, and eta) and heavy mesons (D and J/psi), and we present the results in a convenient form factor length scale. Our findings indicate that the elastic shape factors of mesons rely significantly on the charge of the meson and are less affected by the temperature and chemical potential. These dependencies vary greatly across different meson types, yielding results that are particularly relevant for the interpretation of heavy quark diffusion coefficients and elastic meson production in heavy ion collisions. Our outcome also highlights the importance of considering the internal structure of mesons, as their elastic form factors exhibit non-trivial temperature and chemical potential dependencies, as observed in recent experiments at RHIC and LHC. Our study further reveals that the variation in elastic shape factors can reach up to 30%, primarily due to the interplay between the internal structure of mesons and their moving within the QCD medium. Our outcomes also demonstrate that heavy mesons behave like high mass scales, with their elastic shape factors governed solely by the quark-gluon plasma properties, in contrast to light mesons whose elastic shape factors are more complicated to understand due to their intermediate mass scale, for which a simple explanation is not available yet. Our analysis also shows that the elastic shape factors of mesons can be explored through real and imaginary parts of the heavy quark potential, and our outcomes indicate that heavy quark potential holds significant information about the internal structure of heavy mesons. A liquid droplet, situated at the center of a conductive frame, is placed between two like-electric field lines and undergoes significant oscillations in response to an externally applied electric field. As the frequency of the field increases, the droplet's motion transitions from steady flow to turbulence. To better understand the implications of this behavior in the presence of suspended particles, we conduct a numerical analysis of the droplet's EHD fan in aerosols. Our findings indicate that the accumulated particles significantly impact the droplet's motion, restricting its flow by 50% or more, and notably, the boundary beyond which the droplet becomes fully obstructed varies depending on the particle load. Additionally, we observe that the droplet's ability to maintain stability in the face of changing external conditions is affected by both the concentration of suspended particles and the characteristics of the frame that contains it. Furthermore, we identify two regime shifts in this behavior: the first occurs as the droplet shifts from a stationary to a moving state, and the second as it transitions from a stable to an unstable condition. A key aspect of this research has practical applications in the development of advanced cooling systems that utilize the EHD effect to manage heat in various technological contexts. To this end, we explore the potential benefits of utilizing this technology in rocket propulsion systems, considering factors such as the need for minimal system footprint and the potential for recycling and reusing propellant resources. A numerical model is introduced to analyze the EHD fan in this context, and it is shown that this technology could be an effective solution for cooling rocket thrusters and managing heat in rocket propulsion systems. Furthermore, this research may also contribute to the understanding of dust dynamics within electrically charged droplets, an aspect that could be useful in various scientific and technical applications. Our analysis of the EHD fan has demonstrated the value of both numerical modeling and first-hand observation in the study of this phenomenon. While this research has primarily focused on droplets composed of water, it is believed that similar behavior could also be observed in droplets made from other types of liquids. Our study indicates that this feature could be applicable to droplets composed of other liquids as well. Effective text understanding across various applications relies on a grasp of negation. Despite its importance, negation comprehension within reading comprehensions remains understudied. To fill this gap, we present CONDAQA, a pioneering Chinese set of reading comprehensions that specifically focuses on negation. Unlike other comprehension datasets, CONDAQA emphasizes the interpretation of negations as a fundamental aspect of text comprehension. Each question in CONDAQA expresses a negated statement, requiring the reasoning of both the original fact and the negation itself to arrive at a comprehensive answer. Our proposed dataset contains 11,000 crafted understanding pairs, consisting of 8,000 basic comprehension pairs and 3,000 complex comprehension pairs that incorporate negations. These comprehension pairs are designed to be challenging for multiple models to achieve high accuracy on the entire set, due to the inherent difficulty of negation within each question. Our results demonstrate that current state-of-the-art models, despite achieving good performance on individual parts of the dataset, still struggle with CONDAQA's complex negation comprehension, with a overall accuracy of only 62.35% according to our standard evaluation metric. To better evaluate the comprehension of each question independently, we introduce a novel negation-aware metric that accounts for the understanding of both the positive and negative components of each comprehension pair. With this new metric, our results show an overall accuracy of 56.35% on CONDAQA, indicating there is still significant room for improvement in the comprehension of negations within reading comprehensions. To facilitate further research on negation comprehension within reading comprehensions, we publicly release our proposed dataset, along with our corresponding evaluation models and protocols. Specifically, we introduce a straightforward rule-based model that achieves 74.10% on the basic comprehension sets and 56.35% on the entire CONDAQA set with the standard metric, but only 82.50% on the complex comprehension sets with our proposed negation-aware metric. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development: quantum annealing proceeds gradually from a simple initial state to a more complex state represented by a Hamiltonian, whereas quenching involves an abrupt transition to the same final state represented by the same Hamiltonian. The two processes converge when the annealing schedule is extremely slow. This convergence is demonstrated by a scenario where quantum annealing and quenching dynamics, using both classical and adiabatic quantum algorithms, all yield the same equilibrium state following annealings to various points in the Hamiltonian's trajectory, known as quantum annealing intervals. These findings suggest that quenching can achieve the same outcome as annealing when the interval is defined dynamically in accordance with the annealing schedule. Notably, this observation holds for at least some systems that are difficult to solve classically, such as exact cover, a problem that includes elements of lattice gas, traveling salesman, and graph coloring. The analogy between quantum annealing intervals and quenching may provide a framework for enhancing the performance of quantum annealing by introducing variations in the transverse magnetic field. Specifically, this might involve adjusting the ratio of driving frequencies to the number of qubits, rather than the driving strength itself, which could offer a more robust means of optimizing quantum annealing. The technology described within this research can be implemented using a variety of quantum processors, including a quantum annealing machine based on a array of superconducting loops connected to a cavity, and we outline the relevant performance characteristics for this type of device. We use radiance data from space to study the wave-tilt statistics of ocean waves during daylight hours. By analyzing approximately 300 days of data from AATSR and GOCI, we found that the method of Cox and Munk, who conducted a pioneering study in 1959, holds up when comparing their results to ours. Their findings of a mean square error of 0.21 for the wave-tilt angle and a Gaussian distribution for the wave slope are also confirmed by our analysis. We found that the standard deviation of 0.25 for the wave-tilt angle can be confirmed using a method that eliminates scenes obscured by land, but the standard deviation for the radial distance of waves from the sun remained difficult to determine due to a limitation in the AATSR's field of view. Our results also revealed that the wave-tilt statistics remain the same whether we look at visible and near-infrared data from AATSR and GOCI or only use the data from AATSR, which measures the solar sky spectrum more accurately than GOCI. Our study confirms the robustness of the method developed by Cox and Munk and confirmed their initial findings more than 50 years after their study was published. Despite some differences in our methods, our results also confirm the wave-tilt statistics found by subsequent researchers. We found that the standard deviation of 0.25 for the wave-tilt angle is the most consistent value determined from different satellite observations of the ocean surface. Our study paves the way for studying how sea surface wave-tilt statistics are affected by wind and sea surface pressure using remotely sensed data. We found that the standard deviation of 0.25 for the wave-tilt angle remains the same even in conditions of strong wind and sea, which may be due to the fact that the radius of curvature of waves does not change as much as we expected under these conditions. Our study also shows that we can determine the standard deviation of 0.25 for the wave-tilt angle more accurately by analyzing all the radiance values in a single scene instead of selecting only the scenes with the brightest sunlight, which is the method used by Cox and Munk and confirmed by our analysis. Our study provides valuable information on the performance of AATSR and GOCI, which involves calculating the gain and offset for each instrument, a step that must be done before analyzing the data from these satellites. Our study also introduces a new method for determining the standard deviation of 0.25 for the wave

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that increased dust has on VSI, focusing on a detailed analysis of a model involving interacting gas and dust phases. By assuming a critical endowment of dust below which the VSI persists, we explore how it affects cooling rates and vertical mixing. Computational simulations reveal that in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, dust endowments with 10^-7 by mass or above could suppress VSI, resulting in enhanced dust settlement and a bimodal dust distribution. However, this outcome may not hold true in the inner regions due to an increased cooling rate, which could allow VSI to persist even with heavier dust loads. These findings imply that dust could play a crucial role in suppressing VSI in protoplanetary disks, potentially offering an explanation for observed particle development and settlement patterns. As a result, these models have implications for our understanding of disk development and the potential for planet formation. As VSI can lead to enhanced dust settlement and a bimodal distribution, with implications for the development of particles in protoplanetary disks, these models can be tested through observations of disk systems using the ALMA telescope. This study provides numerical evidence for the recently proposed Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum in simulations of turbulent flows between rotating horizontal cylinders, specifically for rotating cylindrical domains with varying levels of rotation. Our previous findings demonstrated that inertial wave turbulence is possible across a wide range of parameters, and here we present a comprehensive analysis of the energy and enstrophy spectra across those same parameter ranges. The results show that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum, characterized by $E(k) \propto k^{2}$ and $\Omega(k) \propto k^{4}$, is a universal phenomenon in these systems, applicable to both weak and strong rotation cases, and we examine the influences of boundary layers and non-buoyancy forces on the spectra. The observed spectra are consistent with theoretical predictions from the weak boundary layer regime, and we estimate the relative importance of boundary layers in real systems based on the size of the gap in rotating cylindrical containers. Our dataset, named Twitch Players, is an open source graph dataset that serves as a testing ground for evaluating the effectiveness of node representation methods in social network analysis. This dataset is derived from the online gaming platform Twitch, specifically targeting its social network, and is comprised of 96 distinct sub-groups, each containing at least 500 active players. The significant aspect of this dataset lies in the fact that the structure of Twitch's social network is prone to rapid fluctuations, given the transient nature of online gaming sessions, thereby presenting a significant challenge for developers to create reliable node representation methods. In order to evaluate the performance of node representation methods, the proximity preservation metric is commonly employed; however, this approach alone is insufficient, as it fails to consider the original purpose of node representation, namely, to preserve and capture the structural roles of nodes within the network. Therefore, we introduce a novel framework for evaluating node representation methods that combines both proximity preservation and structural role-based accuracy, and we demonstrate the utility of this framework by conducting a systematic evaluation of different node representation methods on the Twitch Players dataset. The evaluation results of our proposed framework are also made available as supplementary material. This approach uses a unique measurement, the elastic modulation signal, obtained from the actuator's elastic element, to create a model-based estimator that pinpoints the system's actual force trajectory. This estimator employs the measured modulation signal and previous force predictions to calculate the unknown external force impacting the system, ultimately yielding an algorithm that adjusts the modulation signal to conform to desired force dynamics. This algorithm is mathematically robust, capable of withstanding bounded disturbances and system errors, and is efficient in reducing force oscillations. The resulting exterior metric is expressed in a form that includes both an anisotropic pressure gradient and a radial acceleration term, resulting in a metric that resembles the Ross-Zundel solution. Additionally, we outline a new approach for solving the Einstein-Field Equations in the exterior region. This approach involves using the known metric features to impose constraints on the fluid's 4-velocity, ultimately allowing us to solve for the potential function. A simple model is applied to analyze the spiral structure's pattern speed. The results indicate that the pattern speed of the bar component is fast, at approximately 75 km/s/kpc, whereas the spiral arms' pattern speeds are significantly slower, ranging from 20-40 km/s/kpc. These speeds are comparable to previous findings in earlier galaxy merger studies. We also identify a small section in the galaxy where a two-arm spiral pattern exists, and calculate its pattern speed to be approximately 30 km/s/kpc. Most current research on grammatical error rectification (GER) has focused on a single domain, utilizing various machine learning models to enhance the accuracy of error correction. Nonetheless, little work exists on adapting models to rectify errors across different languages or writing styles, particularly with limited data available. In this study, we classify languages into two categories - related and unrelated - based on their script type and consider nine diverse languages as target domains. We utilize a related domain as a source domain and evaluate the performance of several models in correcting errors in the source and five unrelated domains, with only 800 sentences at their disposal. The results show that both the transformer-based model and the data-driven model achieve higher accuracy in related domains (94.6 for transformers, 94.3 for data-driven models) than in unrelated domains (85.8 for transformers, 84.4 for data-driven models). Moreover, we observe a significant gap between the accuracy achieved with and without meta-learning in the unrelated domains, indicating that meta-learning plays a crucial role in domain transfer. To facilitate further research, we have made the nine language targets and the proposed approach publicly available. The leading meta-learning-based architecture we present has been found to effectively reduce the gap between training and testing, with only 20% of the original data required to achieve 86.3% accuracy in an unrelated target domain. This discovery paves the way for the development of versatile models capable of accurately correcting grammatical errors with minimal training across numerous language targets. In addition, our research involves a comprehensive analysis of 14,000 tested sentences obtained from the FLORE lens dataset and the sale of 9-target language datasets on the Gigafry platform. Researchers and survey takers often encounter surveys that ask for estimates of expensive items like prices or quantities, which are rounded to the nearest integer. A common assumption is made here to establish a mathematical framework for evaluating survey accuracy - specifically, it's assumed that respondents base their answers on the nearest multiple of a set value (likely $1) representing a range of possible answers. This framework is employed to assess the accuracy of surveys that provide average rounded to the nearest integer when estimating totals, a technique known as the method of equal proportions (MEP). Four scenarios are examined using this framework: MEP is shown to be an optimal strategy when respondents aim to minimize the absolute error in estimates, but it's not the only one; a scenario is identified in which the worst-case absolute error exceeds the worst-case squared error; estimating averages rather than totals doesn't offer a significant advantage; and a scenario in which the best-case relative error is better than the best-case absolute error. Furthermore, it's observed that the best and worst-case errors for individual items can be very high, but these peaks tend to decline as we consider more substantial aggregates of data, indicating that surveys using the nearest integer to estimate totals or averages are generally acceptable for large groups of items. A new method is proposed for evaluating the accuracy of these types of surveys, which involves comparing the estimated average to a range of possible values rather than a fixed value, and this approach is applied to three real-world data sets involving price estimates. It's discovered that when respondents have some level of uncertainty in their judgments, the estimated averages are significantly superior to the actual totals, while the worst-case absolute errors are still significantly higher than the worst-case squared errors. Additionally, the proposed method is useful for identifying outliers based on the accuracy of their estimates alone, a function that isn't provided by standard survey analysis techniques. A key factor influencing the accuracy of these types of surveys is the level of ambiguity in respondents' judgments, and it's shown that when there's some level of uncertainty in their judgments, the estimated averages are superior to the actual totals, but the worst-case absolute errors are still higher than the worst-case squared errors. A novel method is introduced for estimating the variance of estimated averages, which involves a novel approach using the average of the squared errors for individual items rather than the standard formula. This new method for variance estimation is found to perform better than the standard approach in two out of three data sets examined, and it accounts for the ambiguity in respondents' judgments, whereas the standard approach does not. In the context of allocating essential items to self-interested agents, we've developed a novel method for a wide range of combinatorial allocation problems. Our approach ensures the existence of pure Nash equilibria in this challenging environment, where agents make rational decisions to maximize their own gains. Furthermore, we've devised an efficient algorithm to identify equilibria that result in fair allocations, meeting specific efficiency and equity criteria, for a broad class of optimization problems, including general integer programs, network flow problems, and general combinatorial problems. Our model and equations can be easily adapted to address various fairness objectives, such as proportional fairness and the Harvey index. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of our methods on real-world instances from the NEFA dataset, observing in some cases equilibria that are twice as fair as allocated loads in optimal social welfare solutions. In addition, we've explored extensions of our model, including multi-item allocation and double-swap, and derived generalizations of existing results for fair allocation. Our code is openly available on GitHub. For a broader impact, we've developed an extended version of our algorithm and equations as a template for user-specifiable combinatorial allocation problems. This template can be used as a starting point for further research on fair allocation in combinatorial markets. We've applied this template to model fair allocation for a broader range of applications, including fair scheduling, fair shortening of graphs, and fair bin packing, and we've left open the question of determining whether the resulting allocation problems have pure Nash equilibria. We've discussed some of these results at the Fairness in Optimization Workshop 2022 at Columbia University and the 2022 ACM Conference on Fair Access. Additionally, we've obtained theoretical results on the fairness of equilibria, demonstrating the existence of equilibria with optimal social welfare and the fact that all pure Nash equilibria result in fair allocations under specific conditions. We've also expanded the biographic dataset Bi-NEFA and explored the application of our model to the COVID-19 pandemic in a fair reassignment problem. We've formed collaborations with researchers from various institutions and we've obtained funding from the National Science Foundation through a grant for fair machine learning. We've presented our work at several conferences, including the 2022 ACM Conference on Fair Access, the 2022 International Conference on Machine Learning, the 2022 Conference on Artificial Intelligence, the 2022 Data Science Conference, the 2022 Optimization Conference, the 2022 Game Theory Conference, the 2022 Economics Conference

In our research, we diverge from the standard approach in unsupervised domain adaptation, which relies on a deterministic function to map source to target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic networks to capture the complexities within each domain. By doing so, we adjust domains by matching the cumulative distribution of data from the source domain, achieving this by correlating source and target features through shared codewords. Our novel method is underpinned by a method that compares and contrasts the Kat\'{e}rnikov distance with the Jensen-Shannon distance, resulting in an amiable solution that efficiently minimizes target domain data usage while maintaining robust performance on the adapted task. Our results demonstrate noteworthy gains in performance compared to conventional methods, particularly those utilizing deterministic maps, across multiple domains and datasets in image classification. Moreover, our proposed approach requires minimal additional computational resources. We believe this research contributes a ground-breaking method for adjusting domains that could serve as a foundation for exploring innovative strategies in other adaptation frameworks. Firstly, we analyzed the sensitivity of paleo-detectors to dark matter scattering and absorption interactions with nuclear charges, expanding on existing research. Traditional methods, such as MLDC and GCDC, have been used to determine these parameters but are not systematically rigorous.  By constructing a model that directly relates the observable timing data to the parameter of interest under specific conditions, we have developed an assessment method that is systematically rigorous.  This method uses a single dimension of variation at a time and evaluates various configurations of the pulsars and their timing spans.  The results from this method are compared to the current understanding of GW150914's parameters and the findings are published in the MLDC-3 catalog.  This approach demonstrates that when the signal-to-noise ratio is low, the best estimate of the parameter is found near the peak of the timing span distribution.  For a signal-to-noise ratio of 3.17, the 95% confidence interval for the log10A parameter is a range of -2.25 to -1.51.  The newly proposed method also identifies the most informative dimension, which in this case is the spin period of the pulsars.  Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our results on future research and the potential for discovering more gravitational waves with a higher sensitivity threshold.  We also examine alternative models that maintain consistency with the current interpretation of gravitational waves and investigate the potential for gravitational waves to be detected directly through pulsar timing arrays. By examining the correlations between two flavor fields within a pion, we gain insight into the spin-flavor structure of the pion. However, extracting these correlations from lattice QCD simulations poses significant computational challenges. In our study, we utilize an exact representation of the pion field operator to directly compute the two-flavor correlations from lattice configurations. By comparing our results with those obtained from a quasi-partitioning technique, we demonstrate the accuracy of our method at a significantly lower computational cost. Furthermore, our method enables the exploration of different interquark distances that would be inaccessible through quasi-partitioning. Additionally, we investigate the correlations within the pion at a range of interquark distances to better understand the spin-flavor properties of this hadron. Our findings suggest that the pion's zero-angle two-flavor correlations are approximately 0.4 times the square of its momentum-dependent value, and that this ratio holds constant across momentum values. Nonetheless, when the interquark distance increases, the ratio drops according to a $r^2$ law, and becomes independent of the momentum. Our results provide a more detailed understanding of the spin-flavor characteristics of the pion and its interquark correlations. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully comprehend the correlations within the pion, particularly at larger interquark distances that are likely related to additional hadron compartments, as envisioned in the quark-compensating model. Ultimately, our findings underscore the significance of examining interquark correlations within hadrons, as they hold the key to a deeper understanding of hadron structure and properties. Nonetheless, our results suggest that the quasi-partitioning technique, while computationally expensive, still yields valuable insights into hadron physics. action, making them unsuitable for applications involving interactions between
agents acting on continuous action spaces. Additionally, existing methods often
require constructing a virtual environment for policy evaluation, which can be
difficult to assemble from real-world data when involving multiple agents.
Our novel positive-free offline learning framework overcomes these limitations,
as it allows models to produce the desired action output and eliminates the need
for a constructed environment. By only utilizing positive data trails, our
technique achieves highly effective results in multiple scenarios and outperforms
the existing state-of-the-art in areas like robotics and video game control. The

Our study focuses on a scenario where an base station (BS) leverages feedback from a mobile device (UE) to optimize its transmission. To facilitate efficient coding, we propose a technique where a universal codebook made of GMMs is used to describe the UE's preferred directions. This approach enables the BS to determine the most relevant codes by evaluating the similarity between the GMM codebook and the desired signal, with the added benefit of providing an interpretable distance metric. Furthermore, we investigate two instances of this technique: one where the GMM codebook mimics the spectrum of the channel, and another where the GMM codebook represents the distribution of the channel. Our results show that the proposed scheme offers superior performance compared to traditional methods. Specifically, we observe that using a GMM codebook in an FDD system yields improvements of up to 1.5 dB in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and 25% increase in multiplexing gain compared to conventional approaches. We also examine two scenarios for encoding, including one inspired by the minimum description length (MDL) principle and another based on relative feedback encoding (RFE). Our findings reveal that these techniques result in significant reductions in feedback data, with an RFE-encoded GMM achieving a 75% decrease in bits compared to an MDL-encoded traditional codebook. Lastly, we investigate various training approaches for the GMM codebook and provide analysis on the performance of these methods. We also explore the application of these techniques to multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) scenarios and examine the benefits of using spatially dependent codebooks. Finally, we discuss the practical implications of adopting these proposed methods within the framework of the widely employed wireless communication standard, LTE. With the adoption of these techniques, we believe that Luther et al.'s recently proposed GMM-based approach can be effectively implemented in real-world systems with minimal enhancements, such as LTE. Consequently, we are confident that the proposed scheme can deliver substantial gains in throughput and reduce feedback data, resulting in a more efficient and reliable communication protocol. In addition, the proposed scheme can provide a reliable communication protocol for real-world systems with minimal modifications to existing infrastructure. We anticipate that this new framework can provide a more accurate model of real-world MIMO systems and may also be applicable to other communication protocols with multiple transmit and receive antennas. The mechanism controlling the metallic versus insulating states of the transition metal oxide V$_2$O$_3$ has been the subject of intense debate for many years.  Recent research indicates that this phenomenon may be explained by a combination of electron correlation and spin-orbit influence, resulting in the observed metal-insulator transition. However, the average thickness of these studies was greater than 5 ML, and thus the impact of surface termination has not been thoroughly determined.  In the present work the focus has been on examining the relationship between surface termination and the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films of a fixed 2.8 ML thickness.  Leff-enhanced photoemission with X-rays revealed a significant variation in the electronic state at the surface (within 5 ML from the surface) in both the metallic and insulating states, with distinct changes in spin and orbital ordering.  On the other hand, the bulk material showed a clear distinction between the metallic and insulating states, with a focus on different occupation levels.  These findings suggest that the surface termination has a significant effect on the electronic properties of these films, potentially offering an avenue for tailoring their functionality.  Furthermore, it has been determined that a specific termination is required in order to obtain the metal-insulator dual-functionality of these films.  The results of this study may also be relevant to other oxide materials that exhibit extensive surface state behavior.  Finally, it is also demonstrated that there is a specific V layer height that results in a stable, insulating state, which may be of interest in the development of half-integer spin devices.  In addition, this study has implications for theoretical models aiming to explain the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$, with particular attention to the need for a more detailed understanding of the surface state effects. We investigated the performance of a coevolutionary genetic algorithm in achieving Nash Equilibrium (NE) in a static Cournot game, with players making decisions based on their individual experiences. To prevent the emergence of dominant strategies that disrupt convergence to NE, we implemented a robust learning approach where the strongest competing strategy is selected for each player. Our results showed that this method promotes convergence to NE across various population sizes and learning rates. Notably, specifying a high mutation rate is not necessary for converging to NE. A secondary experiment examined the impact of a less rigorous learning rule, which allows for mutations and variations in player decisions, and found that it fails to prevent the emergence of dominant strategies, resulting in reduced convergence to NE. In contrast, the strong competing strategy algorithm consistently yields high NE convergence rates. A numerical analysis of the time required to reach NE in relation to population size and learning rate revealed that these factors contribute inversely to the convergence time. Additionally, a comparison with a traditional genetic algorithm using a proxy objective function showed that the coevolutionary approach yields superior NE convergence rates. These results suggest that coevolutionary genetic algorithms are an effective means of establishing Nash Equilibrium in games via evolutionary learning. Furthermore, the simplicity and flexibility of these algorithms make them a valuable tool for analyzing dynamic evolutionary game dynamics. To facilitate replication and further research, the source code for the described experiments has been made publicly available. Moreover, we introduce an innovative visual representation to illustrate the convergence of players' strategies in the Cournot game. This novel graphical method offers a practical approach for assessing the degree of convergence to NE by means of a Nash Convergence Index (NCI). The NCI provides a clear and standardized visual outcome for convergence evaluation, encompassing both the presence or absence of dominant strategies and the resulting gameplay. However, the manual creation and maintenance of these resources are time-consuming and vast amounts of relevant information stored in online texts remain unutilized. Currently, research focuses largely on leveraging NLP techniques for ontology population, but neglects the importance of updating and expanding existing ontologies to reflect real-world changes and adaptations. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel deep learning-based approach, called OntoRefine, capable of enhancing existing ontologies by incorporating relevant information from unstructured text. By combining a contextualized language model with a graph-based method, OntoRefine can extract context-specific information and match target ontologies to the underlying graph structure, thereby facilitating effective refinement. Our model's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on the Wikipedia dataset, where we successfully improve the precision of existing ontologies by over 15% and the overall F1 score by over 10%. Furthermore, OntoRefine's ability to efficiently process large datasets and handle out-of-vocabulary words makes it a scalable and practical solution for large-scale ontology refinement. Our code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/wh183915436/OntoRefine. In particular, we expect our work to contribute significantly to the creation of contextualized multi-class extraction models, where information is extracted based on context rather than solely on keyword matches. Our innovative approach to negation scope detection, where the scope of negation is determined by both a deep learning-based model and a logical rule, may also serve as a role model for other natural language processing tasks involving complex syntax and semantics. The model was subsequently applied to a complete graph, resulting in the derivation of equations that describe the time-evolving behavior of the average magnetization. A key phase shift from balanced to unbalanced behavior occurs at a critical value of $p=1$ for the complete graph. Additionally, the existence of unbalanced states is confirmed through numerical simulations on random graphs, where the location of the phase transition appears to be influenced by the average degree $k$. Notably, the phase transition in graphs with high connectivity ($k\gtrsim 1$) is thought to occur at $p=2^2=4$, while low-connectivity graphs may require a much higher value of $p$. The presented findings provide a foundation for further exploration of the Ising model on complex networks to understand its behavior in a wider context. This paper proposes a new method for creating a shared semantic space that is consistent across languages. We utilize non-negative matrix factorization in conjunction with two types of constraints - lexical semantic constraints and structural constraints - to achieve this goal. To establish a shared semantic space, we utilize the existing translations to map representations from multiple languages into a single coordinate system. This is done by combining the monolingual representations using a technique that respects the structure of each language's vocabulary. We applied this approach to two language pairs - English-French and English-German - using two large corpora, and the results showed that our method produces representations that accurately reflect the semantic structures of each language, in line with the expectations of cross-lingual knowledge sharing. Moreover, our approach was found to be more efficient in capturing the semantics of infrequent words compared to other methods. The word similarity rankings we obtained also outperformed the existing state-of-the-art methods in 11 out of 13 English-French evaluations and 10 out of 13 English-German evaluations, matching the best scores reported to date. Furthermore, our method produced the top performance in an English-to-French zero-shot learning task, verifying the efficacy of our approach in practicing cross-lingual knowledge sharing. The implementations of our method for word representation learning were made available online. Moreover, we introduced a novel evaluation framework that combines the precision of a knowledge base to assess the word representations' quality, and employed it to assess the representations produced by our method, along with five other methods, using the Wikipedia knowledge base in three languages. The results showed that our approach yielded the most accurate representations in two languages and the second-most accurate in the third. Additionally, the rankings obtained from our method and four other methods were found to be highly correlated, indicating a strong similarity in the semantic structures they capture. On the other hand, the representations produced by the two other methods were found to be suboptimal in this regard. The contemporary state-of-the-art models, notably three types of transformer-based models, were found to generate representations that, while effective in certain tasks, failed to meet the standards of our rigorous evaluation based on the precision of a knowledge base. Additionally, the results showed that the representations produced by our method were more accurate than these state-of-the-art models in two languages and matched their performance in the third. The achievements of our method in three evaluation criteria - the precision of a knowledge base, zero-shot learning, and word similarity - established a new high bar for all other methods.
