The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains extensive annotation inaccuracies that impede the robust training of models. This paper highlights the problematic issues in this dataset and devise the Label Imperfection Analysis Dataset (LIAD) to examine the effects of such inaccuracies on model performance. LIAD goes through a rigorous filtering process to ensure it only includes challenging examples with both erroneous labels and plausible annotation intentions. Our evaluation indicates that many annotation flaws in the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset would lead models to achieve perfect performance on purportedly difficult instances, yet these models would struggle with accuracy on other, previously unseen challenging examples. To rectify this issue, we introduce the Label Imperfection Analysis Dataset (LIAD) which comprises a diverse range of challenging dialogue state tracking scenarios that are resistant to overfitting and provides the ASSIST data set that incorporates both commonly and rarely encountered types of annotation flaws. Our study shows that models trained on ASSIST data outperform those trained on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset across various evaluation metrics. This study is an initial attempt to examine the effects of inaccurate labels on dialogue state tracking and provide a challenging dataset that is resistant to overfitting, allowing for the exploration of robust dialogue state tracking models. This study is an ongoing effort and the LIAD data set, along with our code and techniques, are made publically available at https://github.com/ghru-yu/assist/. Models trained on the LIAD data set also have been uploaded to https://www.internationalconferenceonmachinelearning.org/datasets/ liad.html for easy download. By comparing observations and simulations at various star formation rates (SFRs), a strong correlation between these quantities and the strength of the Brackett-$\gamma$ absorption line is demonstrated. This relationship holds true even when considering uncertainties and potential biases. As a result, Brackett-$\gamma$ can be used as a reliable standard to evaluate the accuracy of SFR estimations derived from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. Our data comprise a comprehensive sample of 332 galaxies spanning from SFR~10$^{-2.4}$~M$_{\odot}$~yr$^{-1}$ to SFR~10~M$_{\odot}$~yr$^{-1}$. Additionally, we examine how the line strength is influenced by other factors such as ionization, dust content, and gas density. Our analysis indicates that within the range of starry galaxy environments, there is a distinct relationship between SFR and Brackett-$\gamma$ strength. Conversely, no clear correlation was found in galaxies with stronger ionization or higher dust content. Furthermore, using a realistic radiative transfer simulation of giant HII regions, we determine the essential components of the HII region contribution to the line strength. Ultimately, this analysis provides a definitive framework for validating the accuracy of SFR estimations obtained from SED fitting using a comprehensive sample of 332 galaxies by comparing their observed Brackett-$\gamma$ line strengths. Additionally, this study incorporates a comprehensive comparison with previous research, including that of Iglesias-Párra et~al. (2017). These agents have applications in autonomous vehicles, robots, and drones that need to navigate between internal states and external environment information. To achieve this, we propose a novel external memory attention mechanism, called VIO, for combined visual-inertial optimization. This innovation allows our framework, EMA-VIA, to effectively utilize both internal state and external sensory input for navigation. Through extensive testing with the EuRoC dataset, we found our method to be more efficient and accurate in benchmark comparisons. Additionally, EMA-VIA outperformed state-of-the-art deep learning-based navigation frameworks on the KITTI dataset, demonstrating its ability to utilize both visual and map information for improved performance. The source code of our method has been made publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, we introduced a new dataset and evaluation protocol for closed-loop visual-inertial navigation, along with a leading model, EMA-VIA*, which set the bar for future research. This new protocol emphasizes the importance of both precise position estimation and robust loop-closure in visual-inertial navigation. With multiple leading models achieving state-of-the-art results on the newly introduced dataset, there is a clear indication that the field of visual-inertial navigation is on the path to performance improvement and future breakthroughs. On one hand, thin models specialize in precise position estimation, while on the other hand, thick models excel in robust loop-closure. The entorhinal cortex serves as a key gateway through which sensory information from the hippocampus is funnelled to the neocortex. The underlying mechanism of the entorhinal grid network, characterized by neuron populations that develop periodic firing patterns in multiple directions, remains somewhat elusive despite being a fundamental component of the hippocampal-hippocampal pathway. This study aims to investigate the properties of grid neurons by examining the dynamics of wave patterns in the entorhinal cortex. Our model features a network of excitatory neurons organised in a grid, interconnected with intrinsic reciprocal inhibitory connections, which facilitates the emergence of stable grid patterns. Through this setup, we observe grid neurons capable of adapting to various environment sizes and spontaneously producing multiple directional firing patterns. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. Notably, we demonstrate the existence of sequences comprising three $S_4$-quartic elliptic curves and one $A_4$-quartic elliptic curve that have a specific rank expansion pattern, thereby exhibiting a complex rank dynamics. Moreover, we establish that given a non-holomorphic Hecke L-function associated with an $S_4$-quartic elliptic curve and its zero at 1/2, the rank of the elliptic curve can be determined for at least three out of the four curves in the sequence. This study investigates the norm of an interpolation operator, specifically one that uses the $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ interpolation to arrive at the $L_2$ space interpolation. The interpolation operator in question interposes the Kullback-Liebler distance between two probability measures within the $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ spaces, ultimately yielding an operator whose norm is bounded in relation to the square root of the Kullback-Liebler distance. This complex operator can be decomposed into elementary operators, each being a component of an interpolation operator that uses the $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ spaces to arrive at the $L_2$ space. These elementary operators can further be expressed as a combination of a classical interpolation operator and a maximum/minimum operator. The analysis of the interpolation operator's norm involves an inequality that can be verified through an examination of the operator's effects on specific functions. The inequality in question establishes a bound for the norm of an interpolation operator that uses the $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ spaces to arrive at the $L_2$ space, with the interposed Kullback-Liebler distance displaying a squared root relationship. The investigation into the interpolation operator's norm also reveals a connection to an entropy-based norm, which is shown to be a topological norm. The study concludes by highlighting potential applications for the inequality, which may be relevant to a broader context involving logarithmic convexity and its connection to interpolation operators.

In contrast, gases with shorter lifetimes, including those of primordial origin like nitrogen and argon, have been preserved in the atmosphere for millions of years. The long atmospheric development on Venus has allowed for continuous operation of the run-away greenhouse effect, a self-sustaining process that has prevented the atmosphere from being lost through solar wind and space. We enhance the existing framework by introducing a contrastive learning technique to harness the information from unlabelled images. By combining domain adaptation and self-supervised segmentation tasks, our method leverages both unlabelled images from the same domain and annotated images from a small number of subjects. With only five annotated subjects per condition, our method outperforms existing baselines using only semi-supervised data with a DSC of 0.9232, compared to 0.8795 for the fully supervised baseline. The polarization properties of extremely powerful laser pulses can be affected as they interact with high-density plasmas, particularly when there is magnetic field present. This phenomenon occurs due to the distinct speeds at which right and left circularly polarized light components propagate through the plasma, resulting in a phase difference between the two polarization components. This phase difference can reach significant levels, even up to 10 π radians, under appropriate conditions of high plasma densities and strong magnetic fields. If the phase difference reaches an odd multiple of π radians, a sudden shift in the polarization state will take place when the laser fully amplifies. We have re-evaluated the electric dipole moment (EDM) of the tau lepton using recent RGE improved determinations of the relevant Yukawa and Higgs boson masses, taking into account uncertainties and interdependencies. By incorporating the new results from FLAMe and STRONG2019, we have derived more precise and correlated constraints on the tau lepton's EDM parameters. Furthermore, we have re-examined the impact of the tau lepton's EDM on its decay, considering the influence of virtual effects and possible intermediate states. Based on these updated findings, we have refined our limits on the EDM's magnitude, with a focus on the imaginary component, which dominates the tau lepton's EDM. Additionally, we have established a new connection between the tau lepton's EDM and its semileptonic transition form factors, which can be probed through rare processes like tau lepton pair production or the elastic scattering of electrons off tau leptons. Building on this relationship, we have developed more precise constraints on the form factors' associated logarithmic enhancements, with an expected influence below the $10^{-3}$ level. Finally, we have investigated the relative importance of new physics contributions from various scenarios, with enteries in the "2" and "3" categories generally dominating the impact on our results. For the real part, the simplest one-loop new physics models usually yield effects beneath the $10^{-3}$ level, with the exception of the new physics involving a scalar state. For the imaginary part, one-loop new physics models can in general yield effects above the $10^{-3}$ level, with the exception of the new physics involving a fermion state. We have also derived more precise constraints on the new physics' contribution to the tau lepton's life time, with an expected influence above the $10^{-3}$ level for most new physics scenarios. Building on these results, we have refined our limits on the new physics' scale and mass parameters, with entries in the "2" and "3" categories usually yielding the largest effects, usually above the $10^{-3}$ level, with the exception of the new physics involving a fermion state for the real part. We have made our results available in a comprehensive new database, with all outcomes presented in the form of plots showing the reach of the CMS and ATLAS experiments at their current level of analysis, and with the expected improvement in analysis sensitivity in the future, as well as with the implementation of the improved FLAMe and STRONG2019 constraints

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a specific error matrix with a particular structure, known as a symmetric rank metric error. This complex matrix is comprised of two identical sub-matrices. We examine two types of codes: those with a binary grid format and those with a Honeycomb structure, both of which achieve enhanced decoding capabilities for this specific error structure. Moreover, this improved performance is shown to occur even when the error matrix is arbitrarily constructed, subject to the aforementioned symmetry condition. We also introduce a new term, the symmetric rank metric weight of a error matrix, which serves as a measure of its complexity and provides insights into the structure of errors that can be corrected by certain codes. Finally, we establish a criterion for correct decoding of codes with the Honeycomb structure and derive a formula for the maximum sustainable density of error sub-matrices for codes with a binary grid format, both of which utilize this new measure. We also extend the field of application of these decoding enhancements to regression problems via rank metric techniques. We introduce a new distance measure, known as the hyperboloid distance, which is a variation of the standard rank metric. We demonstrate that this novel distance yields more efficient decoding performance for small error sub-matrices, even when the original rank metric is employed. This results in the ability to correct three-dimensional error sub-matrices in codes with a binary grid format, and even larger sub-matrices in codes with a Honeycomb structure. This breakthrough enables the correction of spherical errors in binary grid codes, which has important implications for the field of computer vision. Additionally, this research on rank metric codes also provides the basis for a groundbreaking proof that yields the largest possible number of a priori independent coordinates for a quadratic formula with a specific structure, known as a Ericson-Skogman matrix, which has significant implications for the field of coding theory. This achievement, in turn, results in the discovery of the largest possible number of a priori independent coordinates for a matrix that represents the hyperboloid distance, which paves the way for even more efficient decoding of rank metric errors in the future. Nonetheless, it is noteworthy that this proposed scheme for decoding symmetric rank metric errors only provides a solution for correct decoding and does not address the aspect of finding the minimum error sub-matrix with the correct rank. Moreover, this proposed scheme is applicable only to codes with a binary grid format or those with a Honeycomb structure, and there is no general formula that can be applied across all possible error sub-matrices

Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. We then extend these training techniques to models that account for foreground contamination, the complexity of which often exceeds our ability to simulate their effects. The results we obtain from these models are promising, showing the neural network's delensing performance surpasses that of the quadratic estimator when the model is trained on data contaminated by foreground effects, matching the performance of the iterative estimator when this contamination is minimal. Furthermore, the improvement in $r$ recovery varies depending on the specific conditions but generally achieves a figure of merit increase of at least a 1.5 times improvement over the quadratic estimator. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye lenses, we propose a technique called "multiplexing." In this method, multiple lobster-eye lenses are arranged in a grid pattern to cover a larger field of view. Each lens is positioned to direct its light towards a specific area on the sensor, allowing for the use of a single sensor across all lenses. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and observations, showing that it can significantly reduce the necessary sensor area while maintaining high detection efficiency. For the X-ray monitor currently being developed for the 1.3 m telescope of the Aperture Mass Telescope (AMT), this technique could enable the use of two large sensors, rather than thousands of pixels. This would greatly simplify the detector system and reduce its overall complexity. To further optimize the system, we are exploring the possibility of dynamically changing the lenses' positioning to adapt to various source types and magnifications. This "reconfigurable" approach could potentially allow for even more substantial reductions in the required sensor area. We are also investigating the potential application of this technique to other X-ray telescopes using lobster-eye lenses. This issue becomes especially pronounced when working with visually complex documents that require both optical character recognition and layout analysis. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel technique called "Document Augmentation through Synthetic Layouts" that uses machine learning to generate artificially designed tables for training models. By leveraging the natural language processing capabilities of pre-trained models like BERT, our approach identifies crucial elements in the document, such as names, dates, and addresses. It then uses this information to create synthetic table structures that are more efficient to label. Through this process, we significantly reduce the cost of data labeling by limiting human input to just the document region of interest. Our results show that this technique achieves high accuracy on visually complex documents, with an F1 score of over 95% for 12 different name tags, outperforming traditional data augmentation methods like data generation and mixing. To facilitate further research, we also introduce DocumentQA, a large-scale question-answering dataset based on real-world documents that includes both natural and artificially designed tables. With over 10,000 questions and answers spanning 12 different name tags and covering all pages of over 6,000 documents, DocumentQA is an extensive resource that can be used to evaluate the performance of visually rich document extraction models. By leveraging synthetic data and efficient human-in-the-loop labeling, we demonstrate that it is possible to train these models with high accuracy at a fraction of the usual cost. Our findings are particularly relevant to applications like document archiving services, search, and summary generation, where accurate extraction is crucial. We also explore the potential for further reducing data labeling costs through the use of autonomous labeling, a technique that eliminates the need for human input. Our results show that this approach is still in its infancy but holds promise for future research. In this study, we re-examine the performance of convolutional neural networks when identifying the types of binary mergers and assessing the accuracy of their predictions. By utilizing a large dataset of simulated gravitational wave signals, we found that a single, multi-filter convolutional neural network was capable of distinguishing between five different merger events with an overall accuracy of 93.6%. Furthermore, when combining information from multiple filters, the network produced precise predictions for key parameters such as mass and compact object types. Our results also highlighted the importance of initializing the network with training data when identifying binary neutron star mergers, due to the similar waveforms resulting from these events. Building upon this discovery, we successfully developed a two-stage convolutional neural network approach that achieves state-of-the-art performance, producing accurate predictions for binary neutron star mergers and demonstrating enhanced robustness in dealing with signal noise. Our research lays the groundwork for the development of advanced real-time analysis tools, capable of providing detailed information about binary compact object events detected through gravitational wave signals. This study is centered on a key problem in optimal control theory, where a key issue in the control of the scallop model has been effectively addressed. The problem involves determining the best way to move a scallop, whose internal dynamics can be influenced by two externally controllable forces. Concurrent memory allocation on GPUs poses significant challenges due to their unique properties, such as memory access patterns and cache behaviors that distinguish them from CPUs. Current memory allocators for GPUs are limited in scope, often tailored to specific applications or programming frameworks, thereby hindering the development of a broad range of applications that could leverage the scalar coprocessors of GPUs. This restriction is further constricted by the absence of a true address space on GPUs, which complicates memory management by requiring a significant amount of extra memory to store metadata. This problem is particularly pronounced in object-oriented programming, where programs comprise objects with inherent identities that dictate their memory allocation and access behaviors. This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a novel concurrent memory allocator that overcomes these obstacles and enables object-oriented programming on GPUs by autonomously managing memory with a reduced amount of extra memory required. Furthermore, DynaSOAr optimizes memory access patterns to accommodate GPU architecture characteristics, such as the organization of memory and caches. This is achieved through a dynamic sizing technique that adapts to different object sizes and the manipulation of memory access patterns to prevent bank conflicts and improve performance. By integrating DynaSOAr, a true address space into the GPU, and a dynamic sizing technique, this work facilitates a broader range of applications that can leverage the scalar capabilities of GPUs. This is demonstrated by applying DynaSOAr to the development of multiple applications, including a matrix object-oriented program where it delivers up to 1.5 times performance improvement compared to CPU-based approaches. This is particularly notable in the context of a real-world use case, where this researcher experienced the limitations of current memory allocators that led to the creation of this novel memory allocator. The development of efficient and high-power electric propulsion systems is crucial for realizing effective space exploration missions. Despite decades of research and development, the performance of these systems has incrementally improved, but surprisingly, there has not been a breakthrough in achieving high efficiency and high power without compromising system stability. This concept, known as the'specific impulse power factor,' remains a fundamental limitation on the efficiency of these systems. In this study, a novel ion propulsion method is proposed, based on the application of a high-power laser in a zigzag cathode to generate a critical mass of highly accelerated ions. This technique leverages the principle of self-induced translucency, made possible by the rapid creation of a relativistic electron layer at the cathode surface, to provide a highly efficient and stable means of propelling ions. In theoretical simulations, this technique achieved a specific impulse of around 500 kilowatt-seconds per gram, coupled with a thrust of 0.85 millinewtons, using a relatively low power input of 100 kilowatts. Notably, this technique enables the simultaneous generation of multiple charges, potentially leading to even more efficient propulsion through the application of a higher power input. Furthermore, this method facilitates the creation of propulsive devices suitable for a range of applications, including the propulsion of solar electric spacecraft in the surface layers of gas giants and the prevention of solar electric spacecraft from sinking into planetary atmospheres due to excessive acceleration. Additionally, this technique may also be utilized to develop a new form of radioisotope propulsion, known as a 'laser heated ion propulsion nuclear battery,' which could significantly improve the efficiency of this type of propulsion system. This novel propulsion method is also proposed for application in the Area of pilot space propulsion applications such as X3 and APEX. This research may also spur the development of new electronic control systems capable of managing the high speeds generated by this technique, leading to a broader impact on the space industry as a whole. This proposed method may tackle the specific impulse power factor challenge and could consequently lead to the creation of more efficient and high-power propulsion systems for space exploration. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen doped rutile TiO2 using density functional theory with a focus on doped arrangements at interstitial N1 and T4 sites.  Results showed that a carbon doped pair at the N1 site forms an on-site sigma bond, whereas at the T4 site, a sigma and a sigma* bond are created, resulting in a nonmagnetic state for both configurations.  For nitrogen at the N1 site, a mixed-spin configuration occurred, with a higher energy level than at the T4 site but still nonmagnetic, and at the T4 site, a carbon-doped triple formed a stable, magnetic ground state with an energy level comparable to the undoped TiO2.  For a carbon-nitrogen doped pair at the N1 site, two nonmagnetic states emerged, with one in a triatomic shape and another in a linear shape with a higher energy level, whereas at the T4 site, a linearly shaped, magnetic ground state occurred for both a carbon-nitrogen doped double and a carbon-nitrogen doped triple.  Additionally, our results showed that a carbon-nitrogen doped pair at the N1 site forms a carbon-nitrogen bond with a bond length similar to that of a carbon-nitrogen bond in a molecule, whereas at the T4 site, the bond length is longer than that of a carbon-nitrogen bond in a molecule but still shorter than that of a titanium-oxygen bond in a TiO2 molecule.  For a carbon-nitrogen doped triple at the T4 site, the bond length is even shorter than that of a carbon-nitrogen bond in a molecule.  We conclude that a carbon-nitrogen doped pair at the T4 site has the most suitable conditions to form a carbon-nitrogen bond with appropriate bond length, making it potentially useful for photovoltaic applications. Furthermore, we suggest that experimental measurement of a carbon-nitrogen doped pair at the T4 site be carried out to confirm our theoretical findings. Bell's palsy is an acute facial paralysis caused by a sudden inflammation of the nerve that controls facial movements. It requires prompt treatment to prevent long-term complications and is often diagnosed through the detection of specific eye movements in a video. Current deep learning-based methods for facial paralysis analysis are typically designed to identify paralysis by recognizing the overall characteristics of a face or particular features. However, these approaches may struggle with eye-centered detection on videos showing normal eye movements. To address this challenge, we propose an original dataset called EBD (Eye-centered Bell's Palsy Dataset) that facilitates the training of a novel eye-centered detection model. By leveraging both visual and temporal information in videos, our proposed network can accurately identify Bell's palsy-based on the distinctive eye movements. Notably, our model excels in differentiating between normal and paralyzed eye movements without requiring extensive data, thus providing a more practical solution for clinical settings. Experimental results demonstrate our model's effectiveness and efficiency, showcasing its potential as a reliable and easy-to-integrate solution for Bell's palsy detection in videos. Furthermore, our analysis offers valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of the proposed network. Building on this research, we've developed an interactive visualization tool that provides an engaging and comprehensive understanding of the curiosity dynamics at play. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for analyzing complex data behaviors and addressing numerous tasks like regression, classification, and signal processing. While Gaussian processes offer an effective way to model real-world phenomena, their conventional squared-exponential kernel-based approach often relies on questionable assumptions about homogeneous signal decay. A significant alternative is the Mat\'ern Gaussian process, which utilizes a smoother kernel that is theoretically justifiable for modeling deterministic data processes. However, existing implementations of the Mat\'ern Gaussian process are limited to their traditional Euclidean domain applications, such as weather prediction and material defect analysis. This work introduces novel Mat\'ern Gaussian process formulations adapted to graph domains, enabling data-driven learning and inference techniques. Specifically, this study provides innovative kernel designs compatible with random walk-based and diffusion-based graph kernels, as well as a framework for determining these kernels' hyperparameters via Bayesian approaches. In addition, this work is enhanced by an accompanying open-source Python library called PyMGP, which provides an accessible and unified framework for working with Mat\'ern Gaussian processes on graphs. Through extensive experiments and evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed models and algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing the potential of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to excel in various graph applications. As a result, this work paves the way for the application of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes in machine learning and signal processing within complex domain structures, such as graphs structured by temporal interdependencies. Finally, this study on Mat\'ern Gaussian processes is also a significant contribution to the broader field of Gaussian process research, addressing an often-overlooked aspect, namely the analysis of Gaussian processes on graphs. This work is a direct outcome of the research conducted in reference [1]. The rapid growth of mobile navigation and ridesharing services has generated substantial amounts of location data, offering a chance to enhance urban road mapping through collaboration between online platforms and municipal authorities. By sharing their daily navigation data, ridesharing vehicles can contribute to the optimal detection of urban roads. However, this poses significant privacy concerns for users. By applying this solution to real-world data from Didi Chuxing in Beijing, we successfully detected over 80% of primary roads, 95% of secondary roads, and even discovered new roads not initially mapped, using only navigation data from one week in October. The results show that our approach is highly efficient and effective in detecting urban roads through collaboration. These problems stem from the algorithms' tendency to rely heavily on superficial characteristics such as vocabulary and over coordinating the scoring of specific phrases. To address these concerns, we propose modifying the algorithms to ignore irrelevant characteristics and integrate more comprehensive features that capture an essay's overall content and structure. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation method capable of accurately identifying and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a dual-stage Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) called W-Net, which combines a primary stage that produces preliminary mask estimates with a secondary stage that refines these masks through a mask-guided sub-pixel regression process. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated program designed to be executed on a decentralized network. To ensure its reliability, a validator is an essential tool. In this work, we introduce HELMHOLTZ, a validation tool specifically tailored for Tezos's Michelson language and its reference implementation. Michelson is a statically-typed language used in the Tezos network, and HLMHZ leverages its type system to detect errors before the program is run. Additionally, Michelson's dynamic nature means that certain refinements will only be resolved during runtime, so HLMHZ includes a set of refinements that are checked statically, ensuring type safety is maintained even in the absence of type information. This technique enables more efficient and reliable error detection. Moreover, users can incorporate custom validators into the system with ease. Our project is an open-source initiative, and we are happy to receive contributions and suggestions from the community. With HLMHZ, developers can leverage its error detection capabilities to create robust and reliable smart contracts for the Tezos network. With its unique combination of static and dynamic typing, and the sophistication of its error handling, we believe that the Tezos Michelson language and its implementation are an ideal foundation for a wide range of innovative blockchain applications. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the precise location and characteristics of tissue displacement resulting from mechanical indentation. However, the high precision required for elastography is impeded by the limited resolution of conventional ultrasound systems in the lateral direction. We introduce a novel synthetic aperture ultrasound technique with a virtual origin that surpasses the lateral resolution limitation. By leveraging the wide aperture and high-frequency sensitivity of a traditional synthetic aperture ultrasound, this virtual origin approach achieves a notably high lateral resolution without the need for an physical origin scan. We evaluate and compare the virtual origin approach to conventional elastography techniques, demonstrating a notable enhancement in precision in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrate the capability of the virtual origin approach to accurately differentiate between soft tissue and hard tissue, the two primary targets for elastography. The results indicate that the virtual origin approach yields a precise and accurate estimation of lateral tissue displacement, potentially enhancing the detection of tissue pathologies in elastography. The feasibility of the virtual origin approach in ultrasound elastography paves the way for the investigation of its potential in other advanced imaging techniques that rely on precise lateral displacement estimation. We anticipate this study to contribute to the development of high-resolution ultrasound systems capable of accurate tissue displacement measurement, a crucial component for elastography and other related techniques. The study also marks the first documented application of the virtual origin synthetic aperture technique in ultrasound elastography, a technique initially introduced by investigators in 2018. We plan to build upon this success by exploring other possibilities of the virtual origin approach in ultrasound system enhancements, with a focus on the development of high-resolution ultrasound systems through the integration of advanced algorithms. We believe the results presented in this study to serve as a foundation for our research on the virtual origin approach, and we look forward to contributing to the development of the next generation of high-resolution ultrasound systems. In multi-task reinforcement learning, achieving optimal performance across all tasks simultaneously is crucial, but most current methods focus only on minimizing individual task errors. We introduce the problem of destructive interference, a common issue that arises when tackling multiple tasks concurrently. This challenge occurs when different tasks induce opposing behaviors as a result of a common learning mechanism. To address this, we develop a novel framework that leverages multiple modular systems to prevent the development of destructive interference. By using separate critics for each task, our proposed method not only mitigates interference but also promotes the discovery of distinct features for each task. Our results demonstrate that our framework outperforms a non-modular control method in multi-task reinforcement learning tasks, particularly those with destructive interference. Characterizing colorectal polyps histology is crucial to determining their potential risk of cancer. This process, called risk assessment, guides clinical decisions on the need for surgical removal or further surveillance. Accurate risk assessment relies on distinguishing between neoplastic and non-neoplastic tissue types within the polyp, as well as assessing the presence and severity of dysplasia. However, this assessment is a complex and nuanced task for even experienced pathologists.

To enhance the performance of deep learning-based imaging analysis, it is essential to have large, high-quality datasets labeled by experts in the specific field. In this context, we present UniToPatho, a unique dataset comprising histological images of colorectal polyps along with their surrounding tissue, stained with hematoxylin and eosin. This dataset was created to facilitate the development of more effective algorithms for identifying neoplastic tissue, assessing dysplasia severity, and classifying polyps as adenomas or carcinomas.

The UniToPatho dataset consists of 9532 $\times$ 512$\times$ 512 pixel$^2$ images, derived from 280 whole-slide images produced by a histopathological scanner. These images represent a variety of appearances, ranging from non-neoplastic to severe dysplasia and carcinoma, captured at different magnification powers (40$\times$, 100$\times$, and 200$\times$). To standardize the assessment criteria, expert pathologists from the University of Turin independently analyzed each image, determining the presence or absence of neoplastic tissue, dysplasia, and carcinoma, and assigning a dysplasia grade according to the Hamburg classification. This resulting dataset incorporates multiple annotations for each image, reflecting the subjective nature of histological assessment.

We conducted several experiments to demonstrate the potential of UniToPatho in evaluating deep learning-based imaging analysis. Notably, we found that while a basic convolutional neural network could identify neoplastic tissue effectively, the same network struggled to differentiate between non-neoplastic and low-grade dysplasia at 100$\times$ magnification. However, by utilizing a more complex network and increasing the magnification power to 200$\times$, we significantly improved these results. Our findings also indicated that dysplasia grading presents a more substantial challenge than identification, with a notable disparity in classification accuracy at 100$\times$ magnification. To facilitate further research, we have made UniToPatho available for download, along with a detailed dataset description that includes labeling guidelines used by expert pathologists

Language barriers pose significant challenges in global communication, and current translation techniques often struggle with switching between spoken and written text. Advanced neural models have made significant progress in translating written text across languages, but similar improvements have not been seen when it comes to spoken words. This lack of advancement means that people who can read but not hear a language may still face significant communication difficulties. For instance, a person who can understand written French but not spoken French may become confused listening to French audio, which includes subtitles they can read. Unfortunately, this person has no way to know what the spoken words are saying unless the subtitles match the text being spoken, which would not account for mistakes made by the translator. This problem highlights the need for voice-to-text translation capabilities that can translate spoken languages into written text, allowing people to easily understand voices in a foreign language. This technique would also enable text-to-speech synthesis based on the translated text, providing a full end-to-end translation service. Although this paper focuses on a specific trio of languages (English-to-French-to-English), it demonstrates the feasibility of the entire voice-to-text-and-speech-synthesis process and offers practical applications for consumers, such as translation software with no need for user input, as well as significant benefits for people with hearing impairments who rely on written subtitles to follow audio in a foreign language. This innovative approach to translation also paves the way for more complex combinations of written and spoken languages to be handled in a similar manner. Given that digital data does not need to be recompiled after each translation update, users can take full advantage of advanced neural model improvements with zero effort, making this technology even more useful over time. This paper introduces a zero-shot voice translation model based on neural multilingual learning techniques, which allows it to translate unseen speech-to-text pairs given it has learned from numerous related written text translations. This model leverages massive datasets of cross-language text by using a system that can convert spoken language into written text and vice versa, ensuring that it can learn from a vast amount of data simultaneously. Although this model shows near-state-of-the-art performance when comparing spoken and written versions of the same language, performance drops when translating spoken French into written English, likely due to the larger vocabulary differences between these two languages. This model achieves this level of translation capability with just two giant datasets, essentially achieving state-of-the-art results with just one dataset for similar speech-to-speech translation tasks. This connection facilitates the computation of specific coefficients within these algebra elements.
